title: Ravens lose both centers to ‘long-term’ injuries
summary: The Ravens’ center situation just keeps getting worse. Baltimore already lost Pro Bowler Tyler Linderbaum in free agency in March. The early favorite to replace him, former Colts backup Danny Pinter, suffered a season-ending injury during camp. 2025 backup Corey Bullock underwent offseason surgery and never really entered the competition before being claimed off waivers […]
full_text: Baltimore Ravens' center #72 Ethan Pocic receives medical attention during the NFL match between the Dallas Cowboys and the Baltimore Ravens at the Maracana Stadium in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on September 27, 2026. (Photo by MAURO PIMENTEL / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images The Ravens’ center situation just keeps getting worse. Baltimore already lost Pro Bowler Tyler Linderbaum in free agency in March. The early favorite to replace him, former Colts backup Danny Pinter, suffered a season-ending injury during camp. 2025 backup Corey Bullock underwent offseason surgery and never really entered the competition before being claimed off waivers during final roster cuts. That left two healthy centers on the Ravens’ roster heading into the regular season. Now, that number is down to zero. Head coach Jesse Minter announced that starter Jovaughn Gwyn (ankle) and backup Ethan Pocic (knee) both suffered “long-term” injuries in Baltimore’s Week 3 win in Brazil, leaving the team without a single true center on their roster. Rookie Vega Ioane, who moved over from right guard to close out Sunday’s game, will prepare to start at center in Week 4, Minter added. His spot would likely be filled by 2025 starter Andrew Vorhees, though the Ravens have plenty of time to make an addition at either position before their next game. Baltimore is still awaiting more details on the injuries to their top two centers, but Minter’s comments indicate that this is not a stopgap situation. For starters, the team needs to add at least one center for depth, and they could consider acquiring a potential starter at center or guard depending on how Ioane takes to his new spot. He held up in his eight high-pressure snaps on Sunday, and a full week of practice with Lamar Jackson will help significantly. Starting-caliber talent is much easier to find at guard than center, especially at this point in the season, so Ioane plus a veteran guard might be the ideal solution. For Gwyn, the injury brings his first season as a starter to a screeching halt. The 27-year-old followed offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford from Atlanta to Baltimore this offseason and emerged as a dark horse to win the Ravens’ center job after Pinter went down. In an ironic echo of Linderbaum’s playing profile in purple and black, Gwyn excelled as a run blocker but struggled in pass protection over his first three starts. There was every chance of him growing into his first starting job in a brand-new offense, but now, he will work his way back to the field – and hope a starting job is still waiting for him if and when he gets there. Pocic, 31, could be dealing with his second major injury in less than a year. He tore his Achilles last December and was still working his way back to 100%, which was one of the reasons he did not win the Ravens’ starting center job. Talk of him potentially replacing Gwyn during the season will be replaced with concern for his career outlook with multiple knee injuries already in his medical history. Minter said that the Ravens would likely move Gwyn and Pocic to injured reserve, which would sideline them for at least four games and open two spots on the 53-man roster. The first-year head coach also indicated that his team came out of Sunday’s game without any other major injury concerns. Defensive tackle Travis Jones went down late in the game (and saved a crucial timeout by getting off the field without help), but Minter said he was “fine” and the injury was “really minor.” Wide receiver Zay Flowers (hamstring), who was on a limited snap count, is coming out of Brazil “really ready to push to be back in there closer to full time,” Left tackle Ronnie Stanley (toe) “will be a lot closer this week,” Minter added, which would return second-year lineman Carson Vinson to the bench after holding up in his first regular-season start on Sunday.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Buffalo Bills set to face another banged-up offensive line
summary: For the fourth time in as many weeks to begin the 2026 NFL season, the Buffalo Bills defensive line will face an opponent with an injury-plagued offensive line. The Patriots announced on Tuesday that they’ve placed veteran right guard Greg Van Roten — who played for the Bills in 2022 — on IR with a […]
full_text: For the fourth time in as many weeks to begin the 2026 NFL season, the Buffalo Bills defensive line will face an opponent with an injury-plagued offensive line. The Patriots announced on Tuesday that they’ve placed veteran right guard Greg Van Roten — who played for the Bills in 2022 — on IR with a thigh injury. Patriots place OL Greg Van Roten on injured reserve and release LB Riley Wilson from the practice squad: https://t.co/YAtHRWGeUn pic.twitter.com/XOLAmZYNme — New England Patriots (@Patriots) September 29, 2026 In Week 1 against the Texans, newly signed right tackle Braden Smith wasn’t available. In Week 2, the Lions had backup center Juice Scruggs in place of the injured Cade Mays. Left guard Christian Mahogany and rookie first-round right tackle did not play against the Bills. In Week 3, the Chargers were down to their third-string left guard, rookie center Jake Slaughter was playing his third NFL game as the replacement to Tyler Biadasz, and Cole Strange subbed in for Trey Pipkins at right guard. Regarding this injury to Van Roten, he was already the replacement for Michael Onwenu. The Patriots starting right guard — who’s darn good — fractured his ankle against the Steelers in Week 2 and was subsequently placed on IR. Ben Brown, a 28-year-old journeyman with 14 career NFL starts and 1,016 snaps since the beginning of 2023, will presumably slide into the right guard spot between second-year pro Jared Wilson at center and grizzled veteran Morgan Moses at right tackle for the club’s Week 4 game against the Bills. Per Fantasy Points Data Suite, Buffalo is sixth in the NFL in defensive pressure rate at 40.3%. Greg Rousseau has played at an All-Pro level through three games. So has Deone Walker. But we should keep everything in perspective regarding the club’s pass rush efforts to date, because the Bills have been afforded the luxury of facing some relatively banged-up offensive lines to begin the 2026 season. And that theme will continue on Sunday against the Patriots.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills release Phidarian Mathis, but expected to retain him
summary: Earlier today, I wrote an article giving my prediction on what I believed the Buffalo Bills would do as a corresponding move to veteran defensive tackle Phidarian Mathis being activated to the 53-man roster after his suspension — turns out no corresponding move was needed. Joe Buscaglia of The Athletic reported the following regarding the […]
full_text: Earlier today, I wrote an article giving my prediction on what I believed the Buffalo Bills would do as a corresponding move to veteran defensive tackle Phidarian Mathis being activated to the 53-man roster after his suspension — turns out no corresponding move was needed. Joe Buscaglia of The Athletic reported the following regarding the roster gymnastics with Mathis: The Bills released DL Phidarian Mathis today, according to the NFL transaction log. He just returned from a 3-game suspension. The Bills are expected to sign Mathis back to the practice squad, according to a source. As a vested veteran, Mathis was not subject to waivers. — Joe Buscaglia (@JoeBuscaglia) September 29, 2026 Now, technically, Mathis is free to sign with any team, but per Buscaglia’s report, the Bills are “expected” to sign him to their practice squad. Therefore, no Ar’maj Reed-Adams to IR or a release of Mike Danna. And frankly, in my article earlier today, I should’ve included the release of Mathis as a potential path for the Bills to take with his suspension now over. Why? Because DeWayne Carter is playing darn good football through three weeks. He has four pressures on 42 pass-rush snaps, three run stops on 40 run-defense reps, six total tackles — one tackle for loss — and has not be credited with a missed tackle to date. He’s appeared on 38.5% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps entering Week 4. Essentially, Carter is playing precisely how the team would’ve hoped Mathis could play in a rotational role in Jim Leonhard’s defense early in the season. And with Mathis not being subjected to waivers after his release, letting him to go now before retaining him on the practice squad was a prudent decision. Releasing Carter would’ve subjected him to waivers right away. After all that, the Bills roster remains at 53.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills Week 3 game balls: Defense rescues a five-turnover afternoon against the Chargers
summary: The Buffalo Bills are 3-0 after beating the Los Angeles Chargers 24-16, but this was hardly the kind of win that sends everyone home feeling comfortable. Buffalo turned the ball over five times, while heading into the game with zero turnovers, and fell behind 10-0. The Bills did not take their first lead until the […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are 3-0 after beating the Los Angeles Chargers 24-16, but this was hardly the kind of win that sends everyone home feeling comfortable. Buffalo turned the ball over five times, while heading into the game with zero turnovers, and fell behind 10-0. The Bills did not take their first lead until the fourth quarter. The defense made sure there was still a game to win. Afterward, head coach Joe Brady handed out two game balls, both to defenders: Greg Rousseau and C.J. Gardner-Johnson. Game ball: Greg Rousseau Groot is making a habit of showing up in this section. Rousseau sacked Justin Herbert twice, giving him two sacks in each of Buffalo’s first three games and six on the season. Only the 3rd player in NFL history to open a season with three straight games of at least two sacks. His impact went well beyond the sack total. Rousseau finished with four tackles for loss and three quarterback hits, constantly making life difficult for a Chargers offense that had plenty of chances to take control. He accounted for both Buffalo sacks on Sunday. Rousseau was already turning heads after his first two games. With another two-sack outing, he gave Buffalo a disruptive presence it could count on even when the offense kept putting the defense back on the field. Game ball: C.J. Gardner-Johnson Gardner-Johnson nearly had two interceptions. A flag wiped out his first, but he made certain the second one counted, stepping in front of Justin Herbert’s pass near the goal line in the fourth quarter. The timing could not have been bigger. Josh Allen had fumbled at his own 28 yard line just three plays earlier. The Chargers had a chance to turn Buffalo’s fifth giveaway into the lead. Instead, Gardner-Johnson gave the ball back to the offense, and Allen ended the ensuing drive with the touchdown that finally put the Bills ahead. Gardner-Johnson played 68 of 69 defensive snaps. That interception was the moment the defense’s persistence became a game changing play. Honorable mentions (yes, even on offense) Let’s be honest: this was not a game that required a lengthy debate over honorable mentions… especially on offense. Five turnovers, four sacks allowed and 10 penalties have a way of thinning the pool of potential players to highlight. Still, two players earned their way onto the list. James Cook is the tricky one. He fumbled on Buffalo’s very first play, helping the Chargers jump out to a lead. You cannot just erase that because of what came later. But what came later was 24 carries for 154 yards and a touchdown, including 95 rushing yards in the second half. His touchdown gave the Bills a two possession lead in the fourth quarter. The opening mistake counts; so does the way he responded to it. DJ Moore caught six passes for 67 yards on a team-high 10 targets. It was not a highlight-reel afternoon for Buffalo’s passing game, but Moore gave Allen an option when the Bills needed to sustain drives, including the third-down conversions Allen mentioned in his post game interview afterward. On this particular day, that is more than enough for an honorable mention. A win with warning signs Allen did not try to dress up the performance afterward. He credited the defense for giving the offense another chance, Cook for running hard and DJ Moore for moving the chains on third down. But his assessment of the turnovers was blunt: “A lot of smoke detectors are going off right now. We got to clean a lot of stuff up.” That’s the right way to leave this one. The Bills found a way to win despite five giveaways, and the two game balls went to players who made that possible. The defense deserves its moment, even as Buffalo knows it cannot keep asking for this kind of rescue.
author: Sara Larson

title: What Buffalo Bills snap counts against the Chargers reveal about their Week 3 win
summary: Buffalo’s line stayed intact but had a difficult afternoon, while James Cook and the defense helped the Bills overcome five turnovers. The Buffalo Bills are 3-0, although Sunday’s 24-16 win over the Los Angeles Chargers did not come easily. Buffalo fell behind 10-0, turned the ball over five times and needed its defense to keep […]
full_text: Buffalo’s line stayed intact but had a difficult afternoon, while James Cook and the defense helped the Bills overcome five turnovers. The Buffalo Bills are 3-0, although Sunday’s 24-16 win over the Los Angeles Chargers did not come easily. Buffalo fell behind 10-0, turned the ball over five times and needed its defense to keep the game close long enough for a fourth-quarter comeback. The snap counts tell part of that story. The Bills ran 66 offensive plays, down from 74 against Detroit in Week 2. Their defense played 69 snaps, up from 65 a week earlier. Special teams accounted for 23 snaps. The offensive line went the distance again For the third straight game, Buffalo’s five starting offensive linemen played every offensive snap. Alec Anderson, Dion Dawkins, Connor McGovern, O’Cyrus Torrence and Spencer Brown were each on the field for all 66 plays, as was Josh Allen. That continuity did not translate into a comfortable day for Allen. The Chargers sacked him four times for a loss of 30 yards. Akeem Mesidor and Khalil Mack had one sack apiece, while Tuli Tuipulotu had two. After two weeks of uninterrupted playing time up front, this was the line’s first real test, and it struggled in pass protection. Allen finished 16 of 26 for 204 yards with two interceptions and no passing touchdowns. Tight ends remained a big part of the plan Dawson Knox led the position group with 46 snaps (70%), followed closely by Dalton Kincaid with 44 (67%). Jackson Hawes played 25 snaps (38%), while K. Latu added three (5%). All four tight ends appeared on offense for the third consecutive week. Among the wide receivers, Khalil Shakir led with 48 snaps (73%), but caught just one pass for six yards on three targets. That gap between playing time and production is one of the more striking numbers in the report. DJ Moore returned to the rotation after leaving the Detroit game in the second quarter and played 42 snaps (64%) against Los Angeles. He was Allen’s most frequent target, catching six of 10 passes thrown his way for 67 yards. Keon Coleman played 32 snaps (48%) and turned one catch into a 37-yard gain; Joshua Palmer played 21 (32%). James Cook was again the workhorse. He played 44 snaps (67%) and carried 24 times for 154 yards and a touchdown, averaging 6.4 yards per attempt. Ty Johnson’s return to the field was another bright spot: in only 15 offensive snaps (23%), he caught all four of his targets for 50 yards. The defense carried the heavier workload Cole Bishop was the only defender to play all 69 snaps. C.J. Gardner-Johnson missed just one, finishing with 68 (99%). Terrel Bernard logged 64 (93%) after playing every defensive snap against Detroit and Houston. Gardner-Johnson’s fourth-quarter interception at the goal line was the biggest defensive play of the afternoon. Maxwell Hairston, Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb each played 56 defensive snaps (81%). Rousseau made particularly good use of his time, recording two sacks, four tackles for loss and three quarterback hits. He accounted for both of Buffalo’s sacks. Another bright spot was Dorian Williams, who led the team with nine total tackles in 52 snaps (75%), while Christian Benford also played 52 snaps. Up front, Deone Walker led the defensive linemen with 48 snaps (70%). Ed Oliver returned after missing Week 2 and played 28 snaps (41%), recording three quarterback hits. DeWayne Carter played 33 snaps (48%). The Bills gave the Chargers opportunities all afternoon, but the defense limited Los Angeles to field goals after halftime and made the stop that mattered most. The playing time reflects a close game that asked more of the defense than it did a week ago.
author: Sara Larson

title: Strong Buffalo Bills defense; or weak Los Angeles Chargers offense?
summary: The Buffalo Bills worked like heck to give the game away against the Los Angeles Chargers. There were ten penalties that included both a negated touchdown and a negated turnover. Josh Allen had a passer rating of 54.0. And who could forget the five turnovers? Somehow, the Chargers were almost entirely unable to translate those […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills worked like heck to give the game away against the Los Angeles Chargers. There were ten penalties that included both a negated touchdown and a negated turnover. Josh Allen had a passer rating of 54.0. And who could forget the five turnovers? Somehow, the Chargers were almost entirely unable to translate those gifts into points. That’s launched a debate online. Was the Bills defense that good? Or were the Chargers offense the suckiest bunch of sucks that ever sucked ? Drive Enders Second drive pic.twitter.com/fJBVEqSrU1 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 29, 2026 We start with the second drive, as the Chargers’ first drive was their only touchdown. That’s a wild end to a sentence when their team had five turnovers to try to get some scores in. After a seven yard gain on first down, a fantastic read by Greg Rousseau created a loss of six. Soapbox alert: TFLs are just as good as sacks and should be treated as such. On 3rd & 9, the Chargers buy Justin Herbert just enough time to get a throw in to a wide open Oronde Gadsden. The pass is a bit high but Gadsden gets his hands on it and drops it. The Bills’ defensive front had a decent rep, but let’s face it the defense was beat here. This drive ended due to a combination of good play (Rousseau) and luck (Gadsden). Fifth drive The third drive ended with a field goal so that’s not really a stop. The fourth ended with a missed field goal. Yes it’s a stop, but a special teams stop. pic.twitter.com/QSFsTgG0wP — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 29, 2026 This drive is a little bit of both as well. Completely failing to get even a chip on Landon Jackson is on the Chargers. The lineman wasn’t occupied elsewhere and puts up a nominal hand that does nothing to slow Jackson down and block the pass. Jackson still times it up and deserves credit, but it’s a mixed bag. Similarly, on the next play the Chargers end up confused and fail to block well at all. The blocking scheme can’t account for everyone even if they were up to the task. But that’s a feather in the cap for Jim Leonhard and the Bills. It’s a great play call to quickly fill what looked like running lanes and swarm to the ball for a stop after a mere yard. On the sack, that’s pretty much all Rousseau’s technique and the Bills doing what they need to do so Herbert has no escape. Eighth drive We jump to the eights as drive six was ended by the clock expiring at the half. The seventh drive was a field goal so therefore not truly stopped. pic.twitter.com/bJ96Yjqfhn — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 29, 2026 This drive ended because of two incomplete passes on second and third down. On first down, the Chargers gained five on a run play that would have set them up nicely to choose their second down play from anywhere in the playbook. But then they got a false start to go back to 2nd & 10, which is where we pick up. On the second down play, the credit is nearly entirely on Davison Igbinosun who is in the right spot to break up the pass. On third down, it’s pressure from Deone Walker after a stunt on the line breaks him loose. Dee Alford also reads the play and gets the pass break up. Despite having his arm clipped, Herbert had the ball in the right area and it’s possible it’s caught if Alford isn’t on top of it. Ninth drive pic.twitter.com/Enzysf2SS5 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 29, 2026 The Chargers were in field goal range and facing a third and manageable. Justin Herbert wanted seven and gambled that C.J. Gardner-Johnson couldn’t close on the ball fast enough. He lost. Tenth drive pic.twitter.com/59j4lH5KGp — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 29, 2026 The second to last drive of the game for the Chargers was a turnover on downs. Yet again we can’t say one way or the other if the Bills’ defense or Chargers’ offense was the true reason for the stall. You can replay the video above if you need, but the bottom line is more of the same of what we’ve seen before. And that leads me too… The Final Straw The Bills defensive front deserves a ton of credit. Routinely disruptive and winning their one-on-one battles, a lot of positive plays come down to them wreaking havoc. That said, the Chargers’ offensive line was routinely off kilter and didn’t do the team any favors. Despite both these things, more than one drive ended because the ball hitting the target’s hands apparently wasn’t good enough. None of this is exactly unusual in the NFL, but the result is the same. We should definitely applaud the Bills defensive for an outstanding effort. That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be cautious about anointing them though. A stronger opponent with better preparation and execution will likely threaten to score more than 16 points.
author: Skarekrow

title: Buffalo Bills HC Joe Brady wants RB Ray Davis more involved on offense
summary: During Monday’s session at the podium with members of the media, Buffalo Bills head coach Joe Brady took a moment to reflect on running back Ray Davis, and his lack of opportunities in the team’s current offense. Against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3, Davis was in for five plays (8%) on offense, while […]
full_text: During Monday’s session at the podium with members of the media, Buffalo Bills head coach Joe Brady took a moment to reflect on running back Ray Davis, and his lack of opportunities in the team’s current offense. Against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3, Davis was in for five plays (8%) on offense, while also seeing time on special teams with five plays (22%) there on Sunday. Davis earned zero touches on those five offensive plays. Meanwhile running back Ty Johnson, just returning to action following a surgical procedure to repair a hamstring injury, saw 15 snaps (23%) on offense, and one snap (4%) on special teams. Johnson didn’t rush the football, but he caught all four targets his way for 50 yards. Evidenced above, Davis, the 2025 NFL All-Pro kick returner who returned 31 kicks for 943 yards and one touchdown, has a new featured role with Buffalo. Last season while taking over the kick-return reigns, Davis still carried the ball on offense 58 times for 275 yards, also catching 10 passes (13 targets) for 86 yards and two touchdowns. Running back James Cook III, last season’s NFL rushing yards champion, is the undisputed lead back for the Bills. However, Cook doesn’t take every snap at the position. Despite that fact, Davis has managed to earn just one carry (for 3 yards) through three games this season. It’s surprising when you consider that third-down specialist Ty Johnson missed Weeks 1 and 2. Are the Bills simply limiting Davis’ touches to keep him fresh for special teams? Perhaps not, as Brady mentioned that “right now, I gotta get Ray playing more, right? Brady went on to say of the situation that ”it’s a reality. He’s too good of a player,” and that ”Ray’s worked his ass off and deserves that” opportunity. By no means should Cook see less snaps given how productive he is even considering any ball-security concerns. With Cook on the field, the team is always one play away from a sprint going the distance for six. Davis, too, brings a unique ability to the team as someone who’s sneaky fast and tough as nails taking contact. During his rookie season in 2024, Davis totaled 113 carries for 442 yards and three touchdowns, also hauling in 17 receptions (19 targets) for 189 yards and three additional touchdowns. Be it as it may that Davis has a new role with the team, there’s plenty of room to get him involved meaningfully on offense. He’s a proven dual-threat player who’s succeeded at every stop and each level of football. In Davis’ three-year career to this point with the Bills, he’s averaged a first down on one out of every four rushing attempts (42 first downs, 172 rushes, per Pro Football Reference ). As a receiver with the Bills, Davis has earned 15 first downs on 27 receptions (32 targets). The Bills may be wise to find reason to get Davis snaps in a complementary role to Cook, apart from third-down situations. It could come as soon as Week 4, if there are lingering concerns about the amount and types of contact quarterback Josh Allen continues absorbing as a runner.
author: Matt Byham

title: The NFL has a “Roughing The Passer” problem, and it’s not the one you think
summary: With 2:51 remaining in the first quarter of the Buffalo Bills victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, Bills edge rusher Gregory Rousseau was called for a roughing the passer penalty for a hit against Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert. On the play, Herbert got rid of the ball as Rousseau was beginning the tackle. The man […]
full_text: With 2:51 remaining in the first quarter of the Buffalo Bills victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, Bills edge rusher Gregory Rousseau was called for a roughing the passer penalty for a hit against Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert. On the play, Herbert got rid of the ball as Rousseau was beginning the tackle. The man affectionately known as “Groot” wrapped his arms around the Charger QB and, as they both fell to the ground, let go of either side of the former Oregon signal-caller. Rousseau landed on Herbert with both his hands no longer touching the quarterback, but due to the league’s emphasis on the so-called “body weight rule”, a 15 yard penalty for roughing the passer was assessed against Buffalo. This play, combined with a play in the Miami/Kansas City game against Patrick Mahomes, led to a firestorm of social media posts outlining the “yeah the rule is dumb, but that’s the correct enforcement of the rule” mantra that has frequently made its rounds in the aftermath of one of these plays. These comments correctly identify that this rule has been on the NFL rulebook since 1995 with an added emphasis since 2018, spurred by an injury to then-Green Bay Packers quarterback Aaron Rodgers. I'm still confused about this "roughing the passer" call. This is textbook. What else is Groot supposed to do? Defenders are taught to tackle who has the ball. At :04, Herbert gets rid of the ball as he's arriving. This is momentum/physics. NOT "roughing the passer". pic.twitter.com/ymRP47ml54 — Renaissance Man (@Billsfandiehard) September 27, 2026 Dear Football Fans, this is a safe space. Do you think this is roughing the passer? pic.twitter.com/h0T39nnJWz — Robert Griffin III (@RGIII) September 27, 2026 Here’s the thing though: They’re wrong and the NFL officials are wrong in their application of the rule in both the above situations. Using the NFL’s official rulebook as posted , the rule applicable for roughing the passer in this instance, in full, is as such: A rushing defender is prohibited from committing such intimidating and punishing acts as “stuffing” a passer into the ground or unnecessarily wrestling or driving him down after the passer has thrown the ball, even if the rusher makes his initial contact with the passer within the one-step limitation provided for in (a) above. When tackling a passer who is in a defenseless posture (i.e. before, during, or after throwing or attempting a pass), a defensive player must not unnecessarily or violently throw him down or land on top of him with all or most of the defender’s weight. Instead, the defensive player must strive to fall to the side of the passer’s body, or to brace his fall with his arms to avoid landing on the passer with all or most of his body weight. One of the challenges in contract law, and by extension rulebooks, is defining what words mean. In describing the intended application of the body weight rule for calling roughing the passer, the NFL Competition Committee utilized two specific terms that matter: “unnecessarily” and “violently”. Instead of leaving the rule to end with the word “weight” in the official rule above, the NFL specifically provided an outline in the final sentence of the rule to give their officials guidance of what should be expected of a defense player to avoid the “unnecessary” and “violently” tags and by extension, the penalty. How do we know the final sentence is designed to create a way to avoid the penalty? The NFL began the final sentence with the word “instead”. “Instead” creates a binary in the hypothetical situations outlined. It’s either one or the other. You cannot have two situations which are connected with the word “instead” and have them both be true at the same time. In the rule, the player either “unnecessarily or violently throw(s) (the quarterback) down or land(s) on top of him with all or most of the defender’s weight” or the defensive player “strive(s) to fall to the side of the passer’s body”, or “brace(s) his fall with his arms to avoid landing on the passer with all or most of his body weight.” The comma immediately followed by the word “or” in the second sentence connects the two items the defender may strive to do in order to create situation #2 (not a penalty) and not situation #1 (a penalty). The only difference between the two situations created in the final two sentences of the rule is that one of them outlines the defender “striving” to either a.) fall to the side of the passer’s body or b.) brace his fall with his arms to avoid landing on the passer with all or most of his body weight. In the other situation, the defender did unnecessarily or violently throw the quarterback down. The NFL is defining “unnecessary” and “violent” through the binary created by their usage of the term “instead” and any challenge to the rule would involve this specific portion of it. If the defender strives to either fall to the side of the quarterback or brace himself with his arms to avoid a full-weighted fall, a flag should not be thrown by the NFL’s own rulebook. In both situations discussed here, the defender strove to brace himself with his arms to avoid a full-weighted fall. Whether the defender does or does not land on the quarterback and what percentage of landed weight is present is irrelevant; the binary is written based upon the observed intent of the defender through two clear actions they may take. This is not a “yeah the rule is dumb, but that’s the rule” situation. If the final sentence of the rule didn’t exist, I’d agree with that. If the word “instead” wasn’t used, I’d agree with that because it would create a resultant rule: regardless of any action prior to landing, the defender landing on the quarterback with most or all of his body weight would constitute a foul. That resultant rule interpretation is the way the referees and the commentators online are viewing the rule, but that’s not the way it’s actually written. Instead, it’s creating a situation where an action from a defender as outlined can create a situation diametrically opposed to the situation that outlines the appropriate time to throw the flag. If you want to get literal, let’s get literal. I won’t bill any hours for this. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!
author: Bruce Nolan

title: What corresponding move will Buffalo Bills make with Phidarian Mathis back on 53-man roster?
summary: The Buffalo Bills have a roster decision to make, and one day to do it. Veteran defensive lineman Phidarian Mathis was added to the active roster yesterday after serving a three-game suspension to start the season. Upon doing so, it started a 48-hour clock to make a corresponding move to stay within the NFL’s roster […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills have a roster decision to make, and one day to do it. Veteran defensive lineman Phidarian Mathis was added to the active roster yesterday after serving a three-game suspension to start the season. Upon doing so, it started a 48-hour clock to make a corresponding move to stay within the NFL’s roster limits. In June, I wrote a piece on Mathis highlighting what I believed would be an emergent season for the veteran because of the more two-gapping nature of Jim Leonhard’s defense — compared to Sean McDermott’s — and Mathis’ brilliance controlling two gaps at Alabama under Nick Saban. In that article, I included a few nuggets from my pre-draft scouting report on Mathis from back in 2022: “ He really anchors well against double teams. Grows roots and is not easily moved…two-gapping skill is next level .” I’d have to believe Leonhard is reasonably thrilled to get the 6’4”, 312-pound Mathis back onto his defense. A month ago, I would’ve first told you that DeWayne Carter would be the easy one defensive tackle for another defensive tackle flip-flop in this scenario. Heck, I didn’t even think Carter would make the team near the end of the third preseason game, but a late-contest injury to rookie defensive tackle Zane Durant likely helped Carter’s cause. And now look at him — quite frankly, Carter’s been awesome through three weeks. He’s not getting waived to make room for Mathis. I don’t see them releasing veteran Mike Danna too. Remember, he was called upon last minute after Ed Oliver’s freak hip injury in warmups before Week 2’s game against the Lions. My assumption is the Bills will IR rookie guard Ar’maj Reed-Adams, who’s been inactive all three weeks to begin the season and has recently dealt with an elbow injury. I adored Reed-Adams the prospect, and his sturdy play in training camp and particularly the preseason led to him making the team as a seventh-round rookie. But with Lloyd Cushenberry the backup center, and Austin Corbett the backup for either guard position, Buffalo is in a fine position when it comes to interior blocking reinforcement. So Reed-Adams to IR is my guess for the corresponding transaction to Mathis’ return to roster. What’s yours?
author: Chris Trapasso

title: How does Josh Allen play the game after a bad outing?
summary: Josh Allen is quite good at football, but contrary to popular belief around Western New York and amongst the collective Bills Mafia brain, he can be human from time to time, and we saw glimpses of it that phenomenon in Buffalo’s 24-16 win over the Chargers in Week 3. Allen was 16-of-26 for 204 yards […]
full_text: Josh Allen is quite good at football, but contrary to popular belief around Western New York and amongst the collective Bills Mafia brain, he can be human from time to time, and we saw glimpses of it that phenomenon in Buffalo’s 24-16 win over the Chargers in Week 3. Allen was 16-of-26 for 204 yards without a passing TD and two interceptions — of course he scored twice on the ground. His passer rating was a lowly 54 against Los Angeles. That got me thinking. How does Allen rebound after what, by his standards, is a bad performance? Since the start of 2020, Allen has had nine regular season games with a passer rating of 60.0 or lower. In the nine games immediately following those contests, Allen had: four games with a passer rating over 100 one game with a passer rating between 90 – 99 two games with a passer rating between 80 – 89 two games with a passer rating between 70 – 79 That means he increased his passer rating in all nine of those games. His averages across those contests were as follows: 24 of 36 (66.9% completion) 271 passing yards 1.89 passing TDs 0.98 INTs 97.5 passer rating If EPA per drop back is your thing — and it is very much en vogue in today’s NFL — I have those figures for you too. I actually like EPA per play more here than just passer rating because it counts every Allen drop back or rush. Of course passer rating does not factor in Allen’s running, which is a big part of his game. I checked all the games since 2020 in which Allen has finished with a negative EPA. He’s had 16 of them. One occurred in his final (full game) regular-season appearance against the Eagles in Week 17 last year, and he was rested for last year’s regular-season finale, so there were 15 follow-up games to check here. Allen had a positive EPA in the 14 of 15 follow-up outings. The average EPA per play in those contests was +0.246. How good is +0.246 EPA per play for a quarterback? During Allen’s MVP season of 2024, his EPA per play was +0.260. The one instance in which his EPA didn’t jump back to the positives after a negative EPA performance did come last season, though. Allen had a negative EPA per play against the Browns in Cleveland then again was in the negatives the following week at home against the Eagles. But by and large, after a down performance, Allen has regularly bounced back in the next game, not just with a good performance, but one that, by EPA per play, has averaged out to elite-level quarterback play. Encouraging news for the Bills regarding their superstar quarterback entering Week 4’s contest against the Patriots.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Kade Pieper
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: IOWA CITY, IA - SEPTEMBER 13: Iowa right guard Kade Pieper (58) as seen before a college football game between the Massachusetts Minutemen and the Iowa Hawkeyes on Sept. 13, 2025, at Kinnick Stadium, in Iowa City, Ia. (Photo by Keith Gillett/Iconsportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Iowa Hawkeyes interior offensive lineman Kade Pieper Bio Kade Pieper (6’4”, 290 lbs.) is the stereotypical farm-boy-turned-offensive-lineman. After literally growing up on a farm in Nebraska, Pieper earned a three star rating playing both sides of the line as a senior. Just before the 2023 season, he flipped his commitment from North Dakota State to Iowa. After redshirting his freshman season, he was a backup his second year. Finally, in 2025, Pieper took over the starting job at right guard as a redshirt sophomore. He performed extremely well, allowing just one sack and ten pressures while drawing a single penalty across 13 games, earning First Team All-American honors. Iowa’s offensive line took home the Joe Moore Award as the best offensive line in the country. Strengths/Weaknesses Pieper is often considered one of, if not the best run blocker in the entire draft, regardless of position. On top of the dominant run blocking, he is an effective pass blocker as well (a pass block grade in the mid to high 70s from PFF). He has that “farm boy strength” and above average athleticism for an interior lineman. He was originally recruited as a tight end, so his mobility allows him to effectively hit the second level. That mobility is largely due to his small frame. At just 290 lbs., he’s one of the lightest interior linemen in this year’s draft. This lack of size combines with his occasional habit of playing high to reduce his functional strength. Pieper will need to work on leverage while fine tuning his pass blocking technique. Projection Pieper is an exceptional athlete with good strength. Interior linemen often fall down draft boards due to positional importance, but Pieper is one that could sneak into the end of the first round. He’ll definitely be a Day 2 pick at the absolute lowest. The Panthers have a ton of cap space invested in the interior of the offensive line, and their starters at guard are expensive and getting old. Though Robert Hunt, the older of the two, only turned 30 last month, the Panthers have seen how important depth at the position has been the last several seasons. Hunt could even be a cap casualty next season, with the team potentially saving $13 million while suffering $10 million in dead cap. If the Panthers truly want to run the football and protect Bryce Young long term, they’ll need to start investing in the interior of the offensive line with higher draft picks instead of just money. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Kade Pieper is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Are you confident in the Bears and their quarterback room?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Now that’s more like it! After having everything that could go wrong go wrong in the rain against the Minnesota Vikings, the Chicago Bears got back […]
full_text: Jan 18, 2026; Chicago, IL, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) warms up while quarterback Tyson Bagent (17) looks on before an NFC Divisional Round game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: David Banks-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Now that’s more like it! After having everything that could go wrong go wrong in the rain against the Minnesota Vikings, the Chicago Bears got back on the winning track against the NFC East-leading Philadelphia Eagles. Most impressive was the quarterback play from 38-year-old third-stringer Case Keenum, who only got the start because Tyson Bagent began the week in concussion protocol and wasn’t fully cleared until Saturday. Normally, when the starting quarterback goes down, a team’s odds of winning decrease. When the QB2 is out and the team moves on to QB number three, their chances of winning drop off drastically. Let’s be real, not all 32 teams in the NFL are happy with their starting quarterback, and most would have to alter the call sheet and game plan if forced to their backup. But the Chicago Bears have three quarterbacks they feel they can win with. Caleb Williams is week to week with a hamstring injury, and he’ll likely miss Sunday’s game against the New York Jets. Head coach Ben Johnson hasn’t named a starter, but he did sound like he has an idea of what he’ll do. “We’ll have a discussion as a coaching staff, and we’ll see where we need to go from here,” he said. “But I said it last week, and I’ll say it again, there was a reason why Tyson ended training camp as our number two quarterback.” “Whether it’s Caleb, whether it’s Tyson, whether it’s Case, we’ve got one of the best quarterback rooms in the NFL and tonight was a reflection of that.” Does Chicago have the best QB room? summary: As the Chicago Bears move into week 4 and the first “quarter” of the season wraps up, it’s a good time to take stock of where they stand. While the season is no longer divisible by four, like in the 16-game season era, it’s still a good spot to stop and reflect on where the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: T.J. Edwards #53 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after intercepting a pass during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Chicago Bears move into week 4 and the first “quarter” of the season wraps up, it’s a good time to take stock of where they stand. While the season is no longer divisible by four, like in the 16-game season era, it’s still a good spot to stop and reflect on where the team is at. Next week will be when those “quarter-season” pieces start popping up. Chicago moved to 2-1 on the season with their Monday Night Football victory. They’ve been yo-yoing in the rankings due to the offensive volatility over the first two weeks of the season. Is this the week things will start to settle down? WCG – Aaron Leming 10. Chicago Bears (2-1) Biggest Surprise Through September: No Caleb Williams… No problem? Despite a disastrous Week 2 that cost the team three to four games with Williams out, Case Keenum helped deliver a winning month. It would have been easy to write the Bears off after last weekend against Minnesota simply. The offense looked anemic; they lost their starting quarterback, and overall, spirits seemed down heading into a pivotal early-season matchup against the undefeated Eagles. Instead, they have ridden two great defensive performances and a lifetime-from-Keenum performance to come out of September at 2-1 and in good shape moving forward. The Athletic – Josh Kendall and Chad Graff 9. Chicago Bears (2-1) Last week: 12 Monday: Beat Eagles 27-7 QB confidence: Who needs Caleb, anyway? If the Giants had waited a day, they might have traded for Case Keenum instead of McCarthy. Keenum started for Chicago on Monday night in place of Caleb Williams (hamstring) and Tyson Bagent (concussion) and torched the Eagles for 247 yards, two passing touchdowns and another on the ground. The 38-year-old was last a regular starter in 2019 in Washington, where he was 1-7 in eight starts. From 2020 to 2023, he split time between Cleveland, Buffalo and Houston but did not see any action in 2024 or 2025. Williams is expected to miss at least two more weeks, but it looks like the Bears will be OK until then. ProFootballTalk – Mike Florio Bears (No. 12; 2-1): They should ride with Case Keenum until Caleb Williams returns. NFL.com – Nick Shook 12. Chicago Bears (16) Who needs Caleb Williams when you have … Case Keenum?! Monday night served as a testament to the value of experience and lasting athletic talent, because they blended perfectly to produce a memorable performance for Keenum, the 38-year-old who diced up the Eagles and propelled Chicago’s offense to a 20-point victory. As impressive as Keenum was, so too was Chicago’s defense, which stifled Philadelphia’s offense, forced three turnovers and ensured the Eagles weren’t going to come close to mounting a comeback. It’s only one win, but it represents a whole lot more for the Bears, who had every reason to lose themselves in self-pity. They instead decided to rise above and drop a hammer on Philadelphia. Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 11. Chicago Bears (2-1, LW: 14) Case Keenum will be the feel-good story from the Bears’ impressive win over the Eagles on Monday night, and rightfully so. A 38-year-old third-string quarterback played a great game. But the Bears’ defense might be much better than expected. In Week 2, they gave up nine points to the Vikings, but that was mostly dismissed because Chicago lost that game. On Monday night the Bears allowed seven points, and had the Eagles’ snap on the final play of the first half been a half-second later, it would have been a shutout. If the Bears’ defense is even above average, the offense will be very good when Caleb Williams returns, or apparently no matter who is playing quarterback. CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 9. Chicago Bears (12) They beat up the Eagles Monday night. The defense played much better, and Case Keenum was sharp in his first start. Maybe they can handle Caleb Williams being out for a month. ESPN – Courtney Cronin/NFL Nation 11. Chicago Bears (2-1) Week 3 result: Beat the Eagles 27-7 Week 3 ranking: 11 Fantasy surprise: WR Kalif Raymond At best, the 11-year veteran was considered a waiver wire add in the preseason given his status at WR108. With a group of Chicago playmakers highlighted by Colston Loveland, Luther Burden III and Rome Odunze, Raymond wasn’t projected to factor into a significant portion of the Bears’ target share, but that went out the window quickly. Through three games, Raymond leads the Bears with 21 targets, which he turned into 19 catches for 214 yards and a touchdown. He has twice been his team’s leading receiver (wins over Carolina and Philadelphia). Raymond ranks 12th among wide receivers in fantasy production (15.5 fantasy points per game), and his production on punt returns adds to his overall fantasy value. — Courtney Cronin USAToday – Nate Davis 9. Chicago Bears (13): Not only did Ben Johnson’s offense barely miss a beat without QB Caleb Williams, Dennis Allen’s defense was also more than up to the task of stifling Philadelphia’s attack. Those Windy City sails remain plenty full even with Williams still up to a month away from returning. What do you think about the Bears’ power rankings placement this week?

title: Bears vs. Eagles Game Balls: Keenum Shines, Defense Has Hope
summary: Eights days after an injury to the team’s starting quarterback, and with thoughts of a possible lost season tormenting fans, the Chicago Bears set out on Monday Night Football to remind everyone that their championship aspirations are going nowhere. In one of the most impressive games of the Ben Johnson era, the Bears annihilated the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after the Chicago Bears defeated the Philadelphia Eagles in the NFL game at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Eights days after an injury to the team’s starting quarterback, and with thoughts of a possible lost season tormenting fans, the Chicago Bears set out on Monday Night Football to remind everyone that their championship aspirations are going nowhere. In one of the most impressive games of the Ben Johnson era, the Bears annihilated the Philadelphia Eagles with a resounding 27-7 victory that put the entire NFL on notice. With Caleb Williams watching from the sideline, and a recently cleared QB Tyson Bagent waiting in line, the Bears’ third-string starter, Case Keenum, stepped into the spotlight and delivered with a skeptical national audience and fan base looking on. But it wasn’t just what the offense was able to do despite being down their superstar quarterback. Dennis Allen’s defense continued to make strides, shutting down the potent Eagles’ offense almost entirely. If it wasn’t for a last second QB sneak before the half, the Eagles would have been held scoreless. It’s a tantalizing thought to consider what this team could become by December and January (and perhaps, beyond). If the defense continues to play this way, and if Williams gets back and stays healthy, the deepest of playoff runs should be the expectation. Let’s get to the game balls. Offense Game Ball: QB Case Keenum Was there any doubt? Keenum turned back the clock and then some. While the Bears’ 38 year old veteran has succeeded at high levels in the past, it’s been a long time. Monday night, in his first start in nearly three years, he delivered everything the team could have hoped for. Credit to Ben Johnson for calling a great game, but players have to execute and Keenum did just that. His 110.8 passer rating was Keenum’s highest since week one of 2019, over seven years ago. In the end, Keenum was 24/34 for 247 yards, two touchdown passes, and zero interceptions. He also rushed for a touchdown as well on a “sucker sneak,” once made famous by Mike Martz while calling the offense for Kurt Warner and the St. Louis Rams. #Bears HC Ben Johnson says this play call — where both guards pull, making it look like the play is going outside when it’s actually a QB sneak — is an old Mike Martz concept. It’s called a “sucker sneak.” Martz called it in the Super Bowl with Kurt Warner. Chicago used it… https://t.co/HbOSEuiihh pic.twitter.com/gOID0XMdeD — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) September 29, 2026 It will be interesting to see who gets the call to start at QB next weekend against the New York Jets. Keenum certainly has the hot hand, but Ben Johnson stated after the game that Bagent remains QB2. We shall see. Defense Game Ball: S Dillon Thieneman Thieneman wins his second game ball of the young season here, and coincidentally, this one was a toss-up between he and the only other player to win a defensive game ball this year – T.J. Edwards. I felt both guys had a massive impact on the game. Edwards sealed the outcome late with an interception, while Thieneman had an interception earlier in the game. However, I’ll give the nod to the rookie based off of some key run stuffs he was part of on the goal line. Most notably, on two of the three plays prior to his interception in the second quarter. On the play immediately after Jalen Hurts was leveled by LB D’Marco Jackson on the sideline, taking Hurts out of the game briefly for concussion testing, Thieneman was able to prevent Saquan Barkley from scoring a touchdown on 2nd and 4 from the 15 yard line. Barkley ran 14 yards before being pushed out of bounds by Thieneman. Dillon Thieneman saves a TD on Saquon Barkley. Then stuffs Saquon at the goal line. Then picks off Andy Dalton on the very next play. This is a rookie by the way. pic.twitter.com/XmzWeZIhsK — Dave (@davebftv) September 29, 2026 Two plays later, Barkley ran off the right guard from the two yard line but was stopped for no gain by Thieneman. This setup the third down play where QB Andy Dalton threw an interception right to Thieneman, ending the drive. None of that happens without the big stops the rookie was able to come up with immediately prior. A touchdown by the Eagles at this moment would have tied the score and completely changed the trajectory of the game. If Thieneman isn’t already being considered for defensive rookie of the year, he should be. While his stats may not jump off the page at first glance, he has had a massive impact in games and often looked like the best player on the field for this improving Bears defense. Bryan Orenchuk and myself will have plenty to say about this game this week on a new episode of Bears Over Beers on Wednesday evening. It will be available on the 2nd City Gridiron YouTube channel or via your favorite podcasting platform. Our 2nd City Gridiron Podcast Channel is available on Apple , Spotify , iHeart , Audacy , and other popular podcast platforms. Who would have received your game balls? Let us know in the comments section below.
author: Ryan Droste

title: 10 Bears Takes: A Ben Johnson First, Case Keenum’s Legendary Night, and more
summary: To put it mildly, last Sunday was nothing short of an early-season disaster for the Chicago Bears. Not only did they lose a game they had multiple chances to win, but they also lost starting quarterback Caleb Williams for the next three to four weeks. As if that wasn’t complicated enough, there was plenty of […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown against the Philadelphia Eagles during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images To put it mildly, last Sunday was nothing short of an early-season disaster for the Chicago Bears. Not only did they lose a game they had multiple chances to win, but they also lost starting quarterback Caleb Williams for the next three to four weeks. As if that wasn’t complicated enough, there was plenty of quarterback shuffling during the week, which ultimately led to 38-year-old veteran Case Keenum getting the start on Monday against a very good Philadelphia Eagles defense. With the Bears already down one game at home, a strong finish to their three-game homestand was needed. Thankfully for the Bears, head coach Ben Johnson dialed up the perfect game plan, and the team delivered a 27-7 victory in front of a home crowd. Keenum was incredible, the offense did their jobs despite a lack of a run game, and the defense came out in the second half in dominating fashion. Following a long week of quarterback talk and simmering on a tough 9-3 loss to the Vikings last Sunday, we’ll work quickly to turn the page before turning our focus to Week 4 on Sunday. All of that and more in Week 3’s 10 Bears Takes. 1. Monday night was the first time in Ben Johnson’s play-calling career that he had a backup quarterback leading his offense. Although Case Keenum ended up receiving the starting nod, the way they got there was more chaotic than last Sunday’s game. There has been much that Johnson hasn’t experienced over his first five years of play calling at the NFL level, but starting a backup quarterback was first for the Bears’ head coach on Monday night. To make matters more complex, his primary backup, Tyson Bagent, entered concussion protocol Tuesday morning after self-reporting symptoms. Despite being officially cleared on Sunday, the team opted to give Keenum the starting nod due to a full week of practice. The mechanics of losing a starting quarterback (for any team) are already a rough process, especially in the first week it happens. For a team’s primary backup quarterback to go down before even taking a snap in practice is almost unheard of. Thankfully, Johnson and his offensive staff have kept three full-time quarterbacks on the roster since last year. Many wondered why Keenum was brought in last offseason, and it was a fair question. Most teams don’t carry three quarterbacks on their roster, and when they do, the third quarterback is usually younger. Not a 38-year-old who was on the verge of retirement before receiving a call from Johnson mid-offseason. While many, including myself, believed that Keenum was a glorified “player’s coach,” having that caliber of player with his experience sitting on the bench and ready to play proved to be a valuable commodity. Just think- if Keenum wasn’t on the roster, Miller Moss might have been making his first career NFL start on Monday night. Otherwise, the team would have been in scramble mode to sign a veteran who did not know the offense. Either option would have been nothing short of a disaster, and considering the situation, it probably should have been. Even if the results don’t show a starting-caliber player like they would have had Caleb Williams not strained his hamstring, the alternatives beyond Keenum would have made Monday night a much less enjoyable experience. It’s becoming more common for teams to lose their starting quarterback for stretches in a season; it’s much less likely for a team to lose two quarterbacks in just over 24 hours. Teams may look at the Bears situation and put a little more value into keeping a third quarterback on the 53-man roster. After all, had Bagent not been cleared, Moss would have needed to be elevated for a second time just for the team to have a backup. Despite many scratching their heads after the team extended Keenum this offseason on a two-year deal, the guaranteed money he’ll receive over the life of that contract was more than paid off following Monday night’s amazing performance. 2. On Sunday morning, ESPN reported that starting quarterback Caleb Williams suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain. Here’s why fans shouldn’t panic too much about an extended return-to-play timeline. If the Bears’ loss and losing their starting quarterback for the foreseeable future wasn’t bad enough, the hot takes from media, fans, and former players on Williams’ reaction to his injury were enough to make even the most patient Bears fans lose their minds. That’s exactly what the lead-up to Week 3 felt like, and to make matters worse, Chicago didn’t play until Monday night. Although NBC Sports’ Mike Florio originally reported Williams’ hamstring strain as a Grade 1, both Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport reported on Sunday morning that the team’s franchise quarterback had indeed suffered a Grade 2 strain, which could keep him out three-to-four weeks. While some fans felt immediate validation for defending Williams all week, others immediately started thinking about how the team could stay afloat if his timeline stretched by a game or two. Here’s my take: Nothing has changed with Williams and his timeline. Considering the backlash surrounding Williams’ injury and reaction, there’s a form of damage control going on through the media from the Bears’ side. That’s not to say that he didn’t suffer a Grade 2 strain, but it could have also reached a point where the team, which is typically very tight-lipped when it comes to anything health-related, decided to fight back and “set the record straight”. Even if Williams has laughed it off and is thick-skinned, the narratives have run wild, and it’s easy to see why the team stepped in and spoke through the media without making a direct statement. Regarding Williams and his timeline, none of the information put out on Sunday is new from the Bears’ standpoint. When Johnson spoke with the media last Monday and said he wasn’t ready to rule out Williams because he’s a quick healer, he was basing that on the information we all have now. I’ve long suspected he would miss at least two weeks, but would push hard to play in the Packers game. Some of the team’s willingness to allow that to happen could revolve around their record coming out of the Jets game. Still, with a modified plan of attack for how Williams operates in the pocket, it’s not out of the question for him to be ready to go for Green Bay. After all, that would be three weeks on the dot post-injury, which technically fits into the timeline given. It should also be noted that the timeline given in ESPN’s report was more of a generalized approach based on past cases, and not so much on Williams himself. The Bears will be smart with his return, but they also have a season to keep afloat, so the balancing act will continue over the next week plus, but make no mistake, nothing that came out Sunday was a surprise to the Bears. Maybe Monday night’s win changes the calculus a bit, but I’m still expecting a return in Green Bay in Week 5. 3. Case Keenum came out firing. He was 5-of-6 for 45 passing yards and a touchdown on the opening drive. He went into the half 15-of-21 for 149 yards, and when the offense needed him to make a play in the second half, he did… Multiple times Heading into Monday night’s game, most Bears fans would have probably told you they thought their team had a shot, but it was going to take a strong run game to be able to support their QB3. Instead, Johnson had Keenum out there firing pass after pass, completing 5-of-6 on the opening drive for a touchdown, and 149 yards overall in the first half. It would have been easy for Johnson to take a more conservative approach in the second half, but the run game struggled to get much of a push for most of the night. Instead of taking a more…
author: Aaron Leming

title: Hot Take Tuesday: The Case Keenum Game
summary: What a phenomenal night. It was a game where Vegas, NFL experts nationwide, and even most (hand-raised) Chicagoans thought it was a long shot that the Chicago Bears could beat the Philadelphia Eagles without 18 in the backfield. We were wrong. I was wrong. In what can only be described as “the Case Keenum game,” […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears talks with the media after defeating the Philadelphia Eagles in the game at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images What a phenomenal night. It was a game where Vegas, NFL experts nationwide, and even most (hand-raised) Chicagoans thought it was a long shot that the Chicago Bears could beat the Philadelphia Eagles without 18 in the backfield. We were wrong. I was wrong. In what can only be described as “the Case Keenum game,” the Bears handled their business and thoroughly defeated the Eagles on Monday Night Football. They did it with QB3. What it was was a work of art. Both Ben Johnson and Dennis Allen provided a masterclass of playcalling. Even with the running game struggling for most of the game, Johnson and his QB3, Case Keenum, were able to control the clock with a crisp passing game that kept the chains moving and kept the Eagles offense off the field. When the Eagles offense did manage to get on the field, Dennis Allen’s defense had them off balance for much of the night. Saquon Barkley had a strong first half of football, but in the second half, the Eagles couldn’t run the football, could barely pass, and were largely stagnant, resulting in zero second-half points. The coaching was flawless. The player execution was near perfection, but for me, none of it compared to Case Keenum. His on-field performance was memorable; what it meant to him, his family, and his career was something of legend. Keenum hadn’t played in a football game since 2023. He hadn’t been a regular on the field since before this decade began. His career was over. He was set to retire, something he would have done after the 2024 season, but Ben Johnson called him up and said, hey, how would you like to be a Chicago Bear? Keenum has always respected and appreciated Johnson and was excited for the opportunity to work with him. So Keenum signed with the Bears on a one-year deal in 2025. It went so well for both sides that Keenum actually re-signed for a 2-year deal in 2026. Keenum knew his role. He wasn’t going to play. He was basically an additional coach in the QB room. He was a mentor to Caleb Williams. If Caleb couldn’t play, capable QB2 Tyson Bagent would be the man. It would take an act of God for Keenum to play. He was good with that. He had accepted that. His role in the NFL had changed. He was more coach than player, even if he still wore the uniform. But then it happened. The durable Caleb Williams injured his hamstring, and a few plays later, Bagent was concussed. The Bears entered week three down to one healthy QB. Yes, Bagent cleared concussion protocol in time to play, but Keenum had handled the practice reps; Keenum had been QB1 all week, and Keenum would get the nod. And he took advantage of that opportunity. 24 of 34, 247 passing yards, 2 passing touchdowns, 1 rushing touchdown, and 0 sacks. Keenum was incredible. It was a part of his life that he had said goodbye to, and yet suddenly, he had one more opportunity to shine, and that opportunity came on national television on Monday Night Football. Keenum took it all in stride. He said all the right things in the interviews and press conferences before the game. He seemed a little nervous, yet somehow at ease all at the same time. But there was one thing that had never happened previously in his career. His children were never old enough to see him play and recognize that their dad was playing in the NFL. Some NFL players have kids at a young age, and that’s part of their NFL experience. Others have them later in their 30s, and when they do, most kids have grown up and know that their dad was an NFL player, but they rarely are in a position where that isn’t in the past tense. I asked Kyle Long about that, and he said it doesn’t even register in his memory; his father, Hall of Famer Howie Long, retired when he was 4. But Keenum’s son and daughter were able to see their father in action. They were able to see him stand tall in the pocket, deliver strikes all over the football field, and even score a touchdown. They saw their father win a football game on Monday Night Football. You could tell the kids were excited, but you could tell it meant something on an entirely different level for Keenum. It was a gift that he never thought he would be able to receive. It was something he never thought he could share with his children. But fate changed all that, and Keenum delivered in a way that we will all remember. Keenum could start against the Jets, and it may not go well, or Keenum could make his way back to the bench with a healthy Tyson Bagent. There is a fairly strong chance that this was Case Keenum’s final game in the NFL. When players have solid but not spectacular careers, players like Keenum usually fade into the horizon. They are the type of players where we go, “What happened to X?” Only to find out that they spent a forgettable year on the Carolina Panthers two years ago, were never re-signed, and faded out of the league. But it makes no headlines. That’s usually how the twilight of a career goes for someone like Keenum. But Keenum got one more opportunity. He had one more chance. He went out there and turned back the clock. He did it for the city. He did it for his coaches. He did it for his teammates. He did it for his family. He did it for himself. “The Case Keenum” Game may not be remembered in many national NFL circles by 2045, but for fans of the Chicago Bears, it’ll go down as a legendary performance that we will never forget.
