title: Cowboys unleash explosive plays, but find ways to self-destruct
summary: The Dallas Cowboys give us happy moments, but they also give us frustrating moments, and it’s rare that they give us so many of those within the same game. Their performance against the Baltimore Ravens was a little bit schizophrenic as they went from an offensive juggernaut to an offense scared of its own shadow. […]
full_text: Photo by Buda Mendes/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys give us happy moments, but they also give us frustrating moments, and it’s rare that they give us so many of those within the same game. Their performance against the Baltimore Ravens was a little bit schizophrenic as they went from an offensive juggernaut to an offense scared of its own shadow. And trying to describe the defense is even harder. Some moments are pure adrenaline and filled with enormous excitement, while others are a straight-up disaster. This game was particularly difficult as it started great, the middle stuff was gut-wrenching, but then they made a run that had the sweet taste of an international victory right at their fingertips. Of course, we all know how it ended, and it has brought us back to the realization that we don’t really know what to think about this football team. Are they good? Are they bad? Are they average? Can they just pick something and stick with it so we aren’t put through this emotional rollercoaster? The tease started with the offense. They looked absolutely sensational at times. Dak Prescott had little difficulty finding CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens over the middle, and all the tight ends were helping out with nice gains. What an incredible throw from Prescott to Lamb on that bomb that completely flipped the field after that amazing goal-line stand. The running game looked revitalized, and they ran some clever plays to get people into space. They were superb. Mostly. That is what makes the bad stuff seem even harder to stomach. And it was most prevalent on the team’s first and last offensive possession of the game. Their first possession started great. They just flew down the field with ease against the Ravens’ defense. The best part was that the drive showcased the resurgent rushing attack, as Javonte Williams couldn’t be stopped. On the drive, Williams ran the ball six times for 44 yards, with one effective run after another. The Ravens’ defense had no answer, so why did the Cowboys decide to start passing the ball when they had second and goal at the one-yard line? It made no sense, and they ultimately settled for a field goal when their plan of throwing it in didn’t work. That early drive letdown would have been a distant memory if they could have punched it in on their last possession. Let’s set the table for that disastrous sequence of events. The Ravens just scored a touchdown to go up 31-28 with 90 seconds left in the game. The mood was complete nervousness. Did the Cowboys have one more drive left in them? The answer turned out to be yes. Kind of. The offense wasted no time. There was a quick 13-yard gain to Ryan Flournoy that took six seconds. That’s a good start. Two plays later, a quick pass went to Lamb, who zig-zagged 14 yards inside the Ravens 40. They were already in Brandon Aubrey range, and there was still 1:14 left with one timeout in their pocket. Another completion went to Flournoy. Now, they were inside the 30 with still over a minute left. Dak faked a pass, kept it, and churned out a good run near the 20, but now there were under 30 seconds left. Things were getting a little dicey again. Then came a gift from the officials. Maybe it was payback for that phantom pass interference called on DaRon Bland earlier in the game. Regardless, Lamb got arm-tied with Ravens’ cornerback Nate Wiggins, and Wiggins got the blame. The result was 1st-and-goal at the two with 23 seconds left. And they still had that timeout. The Cowboys had this in the bag. So we thought. What happened next is hard to describe. They ran a fade to Pickens. No dice. Then, Luke Schoonmaker got antsy and moved early, causing them to be backed up five yards for a false start. On the next play, Dak eluded pressure and took off, but only for a short gain. One last chance. On third down, they tried another fade to Pickens, only this time Prescott airmailed so high that no catch radius could have hauled that pass in. He didn’t even give him a chance. What was that about? The Cowboys’ immensely talented offense opted to wave the white flag and play for overtime when their defense had been abused and completely decimated with injuries. This supposed greatest offense there is turned into the most scared, hesitant offense there is. GOTI had become SHOTI. Of course, they never made it to overtime because of what happened next, but before we get to that, let’s talk about some of the great stuff the defense did, because they deserve some credit. Those short-yardage stops were incredible. Anytime it feels like we might be overhyping rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham a smidge, he shoots through and smashes any notion that you could oversell his value to this defense. What an incredible player. The Cowboys showed up not once, not twice, but three times on short-yardage plays to make stops. The fourth-down stop early in the game was amazing. Otito Ogbannia and Jonathan Bullard stonewalled the Ravens offensive line, causing Derrick Henry to run right into their backs. With nowhere to go, he tried to slide left, but Donovan Ezeiruaku and Caleb Downs were right there to ensure that didn’t happen. On the goal line stand, both Ezeiruaku and Barham shot through the line and met Henry three yards into the backfield. Henry never stood a chance. And on another play that isn’t talked about as much, Barham blasted through the tight end and started tackling Henry while still engaged in the block. It was an incredible sight. And that was a huge play. The Cowboys had just jumped ahead to take the lead, but they hadn’t shown any signs of slowing down the Ravens offense, so forcing a three-and-out midway through the fourth quarter felt like a complete shift in momentum. Those plays were great, but there were so many times when the defense struggled and was constantly giving up big plays. They couldn’t set the edge, and the Ravens punished them. Designed or not, Lamar Jackson saw holes and took off. They repeatedly gave up big runs along the edge as defenders couldn’t keep runners contained to the inside. The defense gave up big passing plays in the secondary as defenders were late rotating. To be fair, a lot of this was put on the team’s depleted secondary . That makes it tough, but failure to keep receivers from running free in open space ultimately was their demise. And we can’t leave without talking about special teams. The Cowboys allowed a blocked FG when Terence Steele abandoned his blocking assignment to react to an edge rusher that appeared to jump early. We’ll never know if Aubrey would have nailed the field goal or not, but no points for Dallas and great field position for the Ravens. Speaking of great field position, not once, but twice, Aubrey shanked a kickoff out of bounds. He is trying hard to dial in those squib kicks and it is creating issues for the returners, but it is creating issues for his own team when he is giving the opposing team the ball at the 40-yard line. There are many things to be pleased with. Prescott continues to roll, and the defense continues to tease us by flashing its upside. But even amidst these showings, this team can’t do what they have failed to do in the past. Win at big moments. They had this game for the taking, but flamed out in the most Cowboys way. And the bad thing is a lot of this could have been avoided. Better play-calling at the goal line and more attention given to fend off the Ravens’ offensive strength would have put them over the top to come away with the win. Until they can show they are capable of that, they’ll always be the team that comes up a tad short.

title: Cowboys turning point: Costly false start opens door for stunning finish
summary: Football is all about momentum. Sometimes those shifts happen quickly and unexpectedly. The Dallas Cowboys were two yards away from taking the lead against the Baltimore Ravens. After fighting back in Brazil, Dallas had an opportunity to finish the game with its offense and make the long journey home with a victory. Instead, a penalty […]
full_text: Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images | Getty Images Football is all about momentum. Sometimes those shifts happen quickly and unexpectedly. The Dallas Cowboys were two yards away from taking the lead against the Baltimore Ravens. After fighting back in Brazil, Dallas had an opportunity to finish the game with its offense and make the long journey home with a victory. Instead, a penalty helped unravel that opportunity, and Baltimore needed just seven seconds to deliver the final blow. Luke Schoonmaker’s false start during Dallas’ final possession stands out as the turning point in the Cowboys’ 34-31 defeat. The penalty pushed the offense away from the goal line at the worst possible moment, beginning a sequence that ended with Dallas settling for a tie and then failing to protect it. A pass-interference penalty against Nate Wiggins had given the Cowboys first-and-goal at the Baltimore two-yard line. After an incomplete pass intended for George Pickens, Schoonmaker moved early. Dallas suddenly needed seven yards instead of two. Prescott scrambled for two yards, then threw incomplete on third down. Brandon Aubrey’s 23-yard field goal tied the score with seven seconds remaining. Five yards might sound like a small setback, but that close to the end zone, it changes the challenge. Baltimore gained more space to defend, while Dallas lost the advantage of the running game threat right at the goal line. A touchdown was still possible, but the Cowboys had made their most important possession harder before the ball was even snapped. The frustration was greater because Dallas had worked so hard to get back into the game. Jaishawn Barham’s fourth-down stop on Derrick Henry had helped keep the Cowboys alive, and the offense followed with a 96-yard touchdown drive. KaVontae Turpin finished it with a nine-yard scoring run to put Dallas ahead 28-24. Those were the kinds of plays that should have provided the foundation for a memorable comeback. Instead, the Cowboys reached their final scoring opportunity and failed to finish it. Schoonmaker’s penalty was costly, but responsibility extended beyond one player. Dallas still had chances afterward, and Brian Schottenheimer acknowledged that he had over-coached Prescott on the third-down throwaway, placing too much emphasis on protecting the field-goal opportunity. Even then, the Cowboys had another chance to recover. Seven seconds remained, and Baltimore needed to move into kicking range. Dallas did not need a spectacular defensive play. It needed to prevent one. Aubrey’s kickoff went for a touchback, leaving all seven seconds available and giving Baltimore possession at its own 35. Lamar Jackson then found Zay Flowers for 27 yards. Flowers went down, Jackson secured a timeout with one second remaining, and Tyler Loop had his opportunity. His 56-yard field goal ended the game. That is what makes this finish so difficult to accept. The Cowboys had an opportunity to take the lead, then an opportunity to force overtime. Both disappeared through a sequence of mistakes that Baltimore was ready to punish. Schoonmaker’s false start began the decisive swing. The stalled possession left the door open, and the completion to Flowers allowed the Ravens to walk through it. Dallas had done enough to give itself a chance to win in Brazil. In the moments that mattered most, it could not finish the job.
author: Mike Poland

title: 2026 NFL Week 4 Power Rankings: Cowboys show fight despite loss
summary: We have a serious amount of data on our hands at this point in the NFL season. Teams are separating themselves in both positive and negative ways, and because it is the NFL we are also still experiencing surprises from all different directions. Unfortunately the Dallas Cowboys dropped a game that seemed to be in […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect We have a serious amount of data on our hands at this point in the NFL season. Teams are separating themselves in both positive and negative ways, and because it is the NFL we are also still experiencing surprises from all different directions. Unfortunately the Dallas Cowboys dropped a game that seemed to be in their hands last week, and as a result it makes calibration of the league as a whole a bit more frustrating than if they’d won. That’s the way it goes sometimes, though. Seeing other teams rise and fall is often a reminder at least of how the league truly is a week-to-week proposition. It is a marathon where overreactions are normal, but those overreactions should at the very least not be taken to mean that they are going to stick for the rest of the season. All of this means… it’s power rankings time. 1 – Buffalo Bills (LW: 1) There is zero doubt that they are the best team in the NFL right now. I’d imagine they all want to see it carry them through February, though. 2 – San Francisco 49ers (LW: 2) No one knows better than us how impossible-to-stop this machine is when it is rolling. They look that way right now. 3 – Kansas City Chiefs (LW: 3) Give KC credit for finding a way to protect Patrick Mahomes and keep him as fresh as possible for the games that matter as they know they will be in them. They are a smooth operation at the moment. 4 – Baltimore Ravens (LW: 8) We obviously know that they are good and knew so last week. It doesn’t make the loss any less frustrating. 5 – Jacksonville Jaguars (LW: 9) Duval has quite the football team on their hands. They could totally win the AFC this year. Trevor Lawrence has found it and it might be Liam Cohen. 6 – Seattle Seahawks (LW: 4) Sam Darnold is back, but this is still the NFL where anything can happen in any given week. Tough loss in the Washington Football Team Bowl. 7 – Chicago Bears (LW: 11) All week long the conversation was how Ben Johnson had never operated as a play-caller without a number one overall pick at quarterback. I think he is okay in that hypothetical now. 8 – Denver Broncos (LW: 15) For some reason I still can’t fully buy in on this team, but the results are what they are. Huge win last week. 9 – Philadelphia Eagles (LW: 5) It sure is fun to hate watch a team lose, isn’t it? 10 – Cincinnati Bengals (LW: 6) I’d imagine they are going to be sore about dropping that one to Pittsburgh. No harm, no foul long-term, though. 11 – Los Angeles Rams (LW: 7) The super mighty Rams are 1-2. This is hardly cause for concern, but it does underscore how the league is a marathon as noted. 12 – Las Vegas Raiders (LW: 17) Good for them! Undefeated! Keep going so we can really believe. 13 – Minnesota Vikings (LW: 12) Look. A win is a win and I really like what they have going on. It is just so strange because they seem to still be figuring it out, on offense at least. Brian Flores is a madman on the other side of the ball, though. Keep stacking ‘em. 14 – Detroit Lions (LW: 19) I’d sell whatever Lions shares I have now, personally. A win is a win as noted, but I’m hardly moved over surviving a close call with the Jets. 15 – New Orleans Saints (LW: 14) This might still be my pick to win the NFC South. They just ran into the mighty buzzsaw (who would have thought!) that is the Las Vegas Raiders. 16 – Dallas Cowboys (LW: 16) Deep sigh. 17 – Carolina Panthers (LW: 13) Losing to Cleveland has to hurt. That is one they are going to want back. 18 – Indianapolis Colts (LW: 27) They survived the 0-3 bowl with a division rival. That is step one. 19 – Pittsburgh Steelers (LW: 22) Look at Mike McCarthy. 20 – Washington Commanders (LW: 28) They easily had the most impressive win of the week in taking down Seattle. I think if the Cowboys had won we’d be talking about how impressive it was for them to dominate Washington the week before given this game… but losing ruins everything. 21 – New York Giants (LW: 21) It honestly speaks more to the low quality of the Titans right now that the Giants beat them. But goodness, New York just can’t catch a break on the injury front. Maybe JJ McCarthy is the answer to all problems?! 22 – New England Patriots (LW: 10) This team is Very Not Good. 23 – Atlanta Falcons (LW: 32) Huge win last week. Maybe they can ride Bijan Robinson the whole way. 24 – Cleveland Browns (LW: 24) If they win on Thursday night then I think we can start taking them a little bit seriously. 25 – Green Bay Packers (LW: 18) Suddenly the Cowboys’ trip to Lambeau Field doesn’t feel so scary. 26 – Houston Texans (LW: 20) See you on Sunday. 27 – Tampa Bay Buccaneers (LW: 23) They are winless and now facing time without their starting quarterback. Not fun. 28 – Los Angeles Chargers (LW: 25) Easily the most disappointing team in the NFL. 29 – New York Jets (LW: 26) They are feisty. I’ll give them that. 30 – Arizona Cardinals (LW: 29) They are not. 31 – Tennessee Titans (LW: 30) They definitely are not. 32 – Miami Dolphins (LW: 31) Who enjoys watching them? ESPN : 15 (LW: 16) Here we go. Fantasy surprise: WR George Pickens Pickens looked great in training camp, and he was the WR12 in our draft rankings. So it’s surprising to see he has not scored or registered a catch for at least 20 yards. His production was better against Baltimore (seven catches, 82 yards), but the Cowboys need to get Pickens involved more. A team that lived on big plays in 2025 hasn’t been as effective on them this year. Pickens is averaging just 9.6 yards per catch, and he has gone five straight games without a touchdown. — Todd Archer NFL.com : 11 (LW: 12) Another bump up. Dallas could have scored a major victory in an international setting if coach Brian Schottenheimer hadn’t micromanaged the end-game situation with an underlying fear of defeat powering his decisions. There were plenty of positives in this game, though: The Cowboys’ maligned defense finally earned a signature stop with a goal-line stand that opened the door for a fourth-quarter comeback, Dak Prescott continued to play at an elite level with both CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, and rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham logged the first significant stop of his pro career. The same problems surfaced in the end, though, when the defense allowed the Ravens to complete a deep pass to set up a walk-off field goal that never should have been on the table in the game’s final second. I suppose it’s a good lesson to learn in the first month of the season. USA Today : 14 (LW: 12) The first drop. Used their last timeout too early Sunday. Shouldn’t have allowed the Ravens a touchback to start their final drive. Forgot to cover WR Zay Flowers. Basically a key breakdown in every phase inside the final 15 seconds of game play. Same old Cowboys? Yahoo : 16 (LW: 17) A slight tick up. How? The Cowboys completely blew the final 23 seconds. They threw it incomplete on first down, then took a false start before second down. On third down, Dak Prescott, despite plenty of time and no pressure, threw it away instead of waiting for George Pickens, who was wide open. Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer confirmed Prescott was throwing it away, for some reason, and took the blame by saying he had been stressing to make sure Dallas didn’t blow the field goal opportunity. “That’s on me,” Schottenheimer said. “I over-coached him.” After taking the tying field goal, the Cowboys kicked off for a touchback, leaving seven seconds on the clock. That’s a bad clock management error because it gave the Ravens enough time to get a completion and a long field goal. Ravens head coach Jesse Minter admitted his team might have decided to go to overtime if there was any less time on the clock. “Honestly, anything less than seven seconds, it would have been really hard to do the play that we did,” Minter said, according to the transcripts. “We may have even just ran the clock out. But [with] seven seconds left, and with the touchback rules,…

title: Cowboys vs Ravens: Brian Schottenheimer leads a disaster-class loss
summary: There are losses that happen because the other team is simply better. Then there are losses where a team spends the final few minutes handing its opponent every opportunity to survive. Sunday’s 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens in Brazil felt like the latter. The Cowboys had the ball at the Baltimore two-yard line with […]
full_text: REUTERS/Brian Snyder | REUTERS There are losses that happen because the other team is simply better. Then there are losses where a team spends the final few minutes handing its opponent every opportunity to survive. Sunday’s 34-31 loss to the Baltimore Ravens in Brazil felt like the latter. The Cowboys had the ball at the Baltimore two-yard line with 23 seconds remaining, a timeout in their pocket and a chance to take the lead. They didn’t score a touchdown. 23 seconds later, the Ravens were celebrating after Tyler Loop drilled a 56-yard field goal at the gun. Plenty went wrong before those final 23 seconds, however. Dallas committed seven penalties for 88 yards, went just 3-for-5 in the red zone and repeatedly found ways to turn promising situations into field goals or empty possessions. Even head coach Brian Schottenheimer admitted afterward that some of the biggest mistakes were his. Asked to grade his performance as a play-caller, Schottenheimer gave himself an “F.” The Cowboys had plenty of opportunities It’s important to establish that Dallas did not get dominated Sunday. The Cowboys gained 415 yards to Baltimore’s 378, held the ball for 30:38 and produced 27 first downs. Dak Prescott threw for 276 yards, CeeDee Lamb had 112 receiving yards, and Javonte Williams ran for 98 yards as Dallas finally got its ground game moving. This was a winnable football game. That’s precisely why the bone-headed mistakes the Cowboys regularly make matter. Dallas’ first possession reached the Baltimore 1-yard line, but instead of handing the ball to Williams after he had a productive drive, the Cowboys called two straight passes. The first fell incomplete. The second resulted in a 9-yard sack. A drive that could have produced seven points produced three. Later, a holding penalty on Terence Steele wiped out a third-down conversion after a big George Pickens catch. The Cowboys eventually had the ensuing 59-yard field goal blocked, and Baltimore immediately drove for a touchdown. These weren’t impossible problems to overcome. They were the kinds of problems good teams don’t make. The play-calling The Cowboys’ tendency to get cute showed up multiple times . Notably, when Jake Ferguson caught a shovel pass that ended in a fumble, another promising possession went nowhere. Dallas had Prescott playing efficiently, Lamb making plays, Pickens contributing, and Williams running the football effectively. The offense didn’t need to reinvent the wheel every time it reached the red zone or found an opportunity to extend a drive. A coach has to understand his playbook, but a head coach also has to understand his personnel well enough to know when the situation calls for creativity and when it calls for trusting the players who have already established an advantage. On Sunday, Schottenheimer didn’t always seem to make that distinction. It seemed like he was hedging between not fully trusting the offense that was on the field and having to be the smartest guy on the sidelines. Overthinking, overcoaching, overreacting. Red-zone offense is still a huge question mark The Cowboys finished 3-for-5 in the red zone, and the two failures were costly because both came in situations where Dallas had a realistic opportunity to take control of the game. It felt like there were at least a dozen moments in this game where that could have happened, but pinpointing these two would-be opportunities highlights the shortcomings. The most consequential sequence came at the end of the game and Dallas at Baltimore’s 22-yard line. A pass interference penalty on Nate Wiggins moved the Cowboys to the two-yard line, giving Dallas first-and-goal with 23 seconds remaining and an opportunity to take the lead. ESPN’s win probability put Dallas at 77.5% at that point. Four downs and a timeout separated the Cowboys from a potential touchdown. Instead, Prescott threw an incomplete pass to Pickens on first down. Then Luke Schoomaker’s false start pushed the Cowboys back five yards. Prescott scrambled for two yards on the next play before throwing the ball away on third down, leaving Brandon Aubrey to attempt a 23-yard field goal with seven seconds remaining. Schottenheimer acknowledged that he had instructed Prescott to take the conservative approach on third down. “I probably over-coached Dak on that one, because we had the points,” Schottenheimer said. “It had to go to GP or throw it away. That’s on me. I over-coached him.” Prescott even admitted afterward that he probably should have held onto the ball longer and left it near the front pylon. That exchange tells you a lot about what went wrong. Schottenheimer was trying to eliminate the possibility of a negative play, but in doing so he also eliminated the opportunity to do what he is paid to do. Win the game. Rather than trusting his quarterback to make the best decision with the game on the line, Schotty attempted to script the outcome too tightly. That is not necessarily a problem on its own. But when combined with the earlier goal-line decisions, the shovel pass and the Cowboys’ repeated tendency to move away from what was working, it begins to look less like an isolated decision and more like a coach struggling to trust his own offense. Lack of urgency People typically mix urgency in football with speed and tempo. That isn’t wrong, but I think a coach like Schottenheimer fails to realize it also means not taking a play for granted. After Aubrey tied the game with seven seconds to go before overtime, the Cowboys avoided the risk of a long return by kicking the touchback, even though they could have burned valuable seconds off the clock. Now to the last offensive play. There is plenty to discuss about the defensive call on that final play, and that responsibility ultimately falls more directly on defensive coordinator Christian Parker. Schottenheimer explained afterward that he liked the defensive call because he wanted the Cowboys to remain aggressive and “sticky” in coverage, which they weren’t, giving up a 27-yard pass to a wide-open Zay Flowers. Tyler Loop then banged home the game-winner. As the head coach, Schottenheimer owns the larger sequence. The Cowboys had just tied the game with seven seconds remaining. Instead of forcing Baltimore to return the kick before attempting a desperation pass, Dallas kicked the ball into the end zone for a touchback, allowing the Ravens to start at their own 35-yard line with all seven seconds remaining. Jackson then needed only one completion to put Baltimore in range. The decision may have made sense within the defensive philosophy the Cowboys had in mind, but in practice and in hindsight, it was foolish. Still, the result was another example of a game where the Cowboys had a chance to control the situation and instead let the opponent dictate it. It really felt like the Cowboys thought the Ravens would just take this game into overtime. If they kept everything in front of them and didn’t give up a touchdown, they’d head to OT with a fresh start. They reckoned there was no way the Ravens would play to win. What now ? The Cowboys did not lose because their offense was incapable of moving the football, or because the defense couldn’t get stops; they had a few. They lost because the team repeatedly struggled to turn that production and those stops into the situational execution that closes games. Schottenheimer must figure out what his offense does best and trust it when the game demands it. If Williams is running effectively, Dallas needs to stay with him. If Lamb and Pickens are winning their matchups, stick with them. The offense should not feel compelled to manufacture something simply because the defense might be expecting the obvious answer. When Prescott has the ball with the game on the line, the coaching staff has to give him just the right amount of guidance to succeed without taking away the instincts that have made him one of the league’s more productive quarterbacks. Schottenheimer deserves credit for…

title: Cowboys rookie report: Jaishawn Barham delivers big in Ravens loss
summary: The Dallas Cowboys’ trip to Brazil ended in frustration, with the Baltimore Ravens winning on a last-second field goal. For the rookie class, there were reasons for encouragement. Caleb Downs helped create an early scoring opportunity, while Jaishawn Barham produced two second-half stops that gave Dallas a chance to take control. The challenge remains turning […]
full_text: Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys’ trip to Brazil ended in frustration, with the Baltimore Ravens winning on a last-second field goal. For the rookie class, there were reasons for encouragement. Caleb Downs helped create an early scoring opportunity, while Jaishawn Barham produced two second-half stops that gave Dallas a chance to take control. The challenge remains turning those individual moments into a complete defensive performance. But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. Caleb Downs (Defensive snaps: 64 | Tackles: 3 | TFL: 0 | Sacks: 0 | INT: 0 | Passes defended: 0) Downs’ biggest contribution came early, stopping Derrick Henry for no gain on fourth-and-one and handing Dallas possession at Baltimore’s 30-yard line. That short field became an important Cowboys touchdown which added weight to Down’s stop. His tackle total was modest, but the importance of that stop was considerable. This was a game with a valuable individual highlight, alongside a couple of things to clean up. Malachi Lawrence (Defensive snaps: 17 | Tackles: 2 | TFL: 0 | Sacks: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | Pressures: 0 | Special-teams tackles: 1) Lawrence assisted on two defensive tackles and contributed a kickoff tackle, but his opportunities to rush Lamar Jackson were limited. He made only three pass-rush snaps, with no pressure generated. That small sample matters when judging the performance as Dallas needs more disruption from its edge defenders, but Lawrence had relatively few chances to provide it. His contribution was mainly supporting the run defense and covering kicks. Jaishawn Barham (Defensive snaps: 50 | Tackles: 7 | TFL: 2 | Sacks: 0 | INT: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | Pressures: 1) Barham provided the strongest rookie performance, particularly when Dallas desperately needed a response. His fourth-and-goal stop against Henry denied Baltimore a touchdown, and another tackle behind the line on the following Ravens possession helped keep the Cowboys in the fight. Those were substantial plays against one of the league’s most difficult runners to bring down. Brian Schottenheimer also praised his command of the defense while handling the green-dot communication duties. There were mistakes alongside the highlights. Barham did make two missed tackles against the run and four completions for 50 yards in coverage. His response was the encouraging part. He continued making decisive plays rather than allowing the difficult moments to define his night. LT Overton (Defensive snaps: 15 | Tackles: 2 | TFL: 0 | Sacks: 0 | INT: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | Pressures: 0) Overton’s limited appearance earned an encouraging initial PFF grade of 77.4. His contribution came against the run, but he generated no pressures on six pass-rush snaps. It was a promising small sample, with pass-rush production still to develop.

title: Bo Nix, fourth quarter comebacks and game-winning drives
summary: The Broncos pulled off another come from behind win, which was amazing for Bronco fans, but terrible for our collective blood pressure. After a poor first half, in which the team was down 16, the Broncos roared back to tie the game at 16. Coming into the game the Broncos were 5-95-1 all-time when trailing […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 27: Denver Broncos safety Talanoa Hufanga (9) leaps before intercepting a last second pass attempt in the fourth quarter during a game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Broncos pulled off another come from behind win, which was amazing for Bronco fans, but terrible for our collective blood pressure. After a poor first half, in which the team was down 16, the Broncos roared back to tie the game at 16. Coming into the game the Broncos were 5-95-1 all-time when trailing by 15 or more at the half. So now the Broncos are 6-95-1. The generally accepted definition of a fourth quarter comeback (4QC) is when a QB leads a scoring drive in the fourth quarter with the team trailing by one score to either take the lead or tie AND the team goes on to win or tie the game. I did not realize until doing the research for this article that it didn’t count as a 4QC if the team ended up losing the game. I distinctly remember a game from 1993 when John Elway and the Broncos faced Joe Montana and the Chiefs. The Broncos were down 24-21 in the 4th until Elway led a TD drive to take a 28-24 lead. Montana then led the Chiefs on a game-winning drive in the final seconds to steal a 31-28 victory. John Elway started 231 regular season games in his career and had 31 4QC and 40 GWD (game winning drives). Tom Brady is the career leader in both categories with 46 and 58, but he didn’t get them very often. This is due to the nature of both stats. If you play for a team with a good defense and a good offense, you are not going to have many chances to lead a 4QC or a GWD. Among Hall of Fame or future HoF QBs, Johnny Unitas has the highest rate of 4QC/GS at 0.186. Brady is at 0.138 which is 8th. If you sort by GWD/GS like my tweet below, Ben Roethlisberger is #1 among HoF (or soon to be HoF) QBs with a rate of 0.215. Tom Brady is 9th. Peyton Manning is 3rd. Most Hall of Fame (or future HoF) QBs did not have to lead game winning drives very often because their teams played with leads often. Big Ben has highest rate at 0.215 GWD/GS. Among active QBs Nix leads at 0.324 (min 16 GS). pic.twitter.com/M5ph9ZzgKj — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) September 29, 2026 Bo Nix has been getting 4QC and GWD at a rate that is astounding and the 2nd best in history for a QB with 20 or more GS. Nix has essentially been leading one GWD every three starts – 32.4 percent of the time. Andrew Luck finished his career at 23.3. Big Ben finished at 21.5. Josh Allen is at 20.8. Matthew Stafford is at 20.7. Peyton Manning is second among current HoF QBs at 20.4. Game winning drives are defined as drives in the 4th quarter or OT that put the team in the lead for good. Future HoFer, Aaron Rodgers, is 125th all time at 14.6 percent. Outside of Vince Young and Bo Nix, most casual fans would not recognize any of the other names in the top 10 below. Maybe they would with Doug Williams since he led Washington to a Super Bowl victory in a game that has been erased from my memory – someone told me they played Denver. Patrick Mahomes is 41st on this list, which, to some, would invalidate this analysis, but it’s more a factor of the vagary of both of these stats. If your team is too bad or too good, you won’t have the opportunity for either. Bo Nix has been in a perfect situation where he can do this and he has been given a multitude of chances to do so in his first two plus seasons as a starter in the NFL. He already has as many GWD as former Bronco, Brian Griese, had in 83 GS. Bo Nix has 37. The hope is that the Bronco offense improves to the point where the Broncos get leads early like the mid-90s Broncos used to, and then hold that lead for the rest of the game. Like Nix, Caleb Williams has also been put in plenty of situations where he needed to lead a 4QC during his young career. He has eight 4QC in 36 GS, which is second to Nix, but interestingly, tied with Kenny Pickett at 0.222. Nix is at 0.270. Among the other big 6, Jayden Daniels is at 0.154 for 4QC and the same for GWD. JJ McCarthy is at 0.100 for both. Drake Maye is at 0.031 and 0.063. Michael Penix has zero of both in 13 career starts. Among active QBs with 30 or more starts, Drake Maye and CJ Stroud have the lowest 4QC percentage at 3.1 and 4.1 percent. I’m not sure how many opportunities these QBs have had for 4QC or GWD, but here are the worst at both among starters with 30 or more GS. What’s unreal is the draft position of those QBs. With the exception of Brissett and Purdy, they are all first round picks and only Mac Jones was late first round. If you just look at passing in the 4th quarter when trailing by one score 2024-2026, Jayden Daniels has the best passer rating at 125.6 and Bo Nix is good, but not great. JJ McCarthy did not have enough throws in these situations to qualify (min 20 throws). He only has 16. I was surprised to see how bad Patrick Mahomes has been in the 4th quarter when trailing by 8 or fewer points over the last two plus seasons. Keeping company with Cam Ward and Anthony Richardson is not good (for the Chiefs).

full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - SEPTEMBER 20: Quarterback Brock Purdy (13) celebrates with tight end George Kittle (85) of the San Francisco 49ers and teammates after a touchdown play against the Miami Dolphins during a game at Levi's Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. This 49ers offense is a tough outing because they are coached to take advantage of scheme mismatches in coverage and punish weak links on defense. Thankfully, the Broncos have a fighter’s chance because their defensive coordinator isn’t too shabby either. Look out for the 9ers beating the drum of matching Kittle on either of our inside linebackers in coverage. Also look out for McCaffrey ever getting to the 2nd level, as he’s going to challenge the tackling capabilities of this defense and is a threat to break a big run at any time. If I’m thinking like Sean Payton about how this game is likely to go, the Broncos are going to need to score points early and often in order to keep up. I don’t think there is a high likelihood of this being a low-scoring game from the 49ers. This would be a great week for the Broncos to figure out how to get their offense on track early for a change. This is just the kind of team that Payton was alluding to when he talked about better teams making it almost impossible for a 2nd-half comeback. If we start the 3rd quarter down 16 – 0 in San Francisco, it is going to be rough sledding to find a way to win against that disciplined and well-rounded team. title: Broncos vs. Rams: The No Bull Review
summary: Don’t you dare count out this Denver Broncos team after one bad half of football. This is still the same Denver Broncos we cheered for last year. This team never stops fighting. The opponent may be absolutely kicking the Broncos up and down the field on both sides of the ball for 2 quarters. Sorry, […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 27: Talanoa Hufanga #9 of the Denver Broncos celebrates as he walks off the field after their 30-26 win against the Los Angeles Rams at Empower Field at Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Don’t you dare count out this Denver Broncos team after one bad half of football. This is still the same Denver Broncos we cheered for last year. This team never stops fighting. The opponent may be absolutely kicking the Broncos up and down the field on both sides of the ball for 2 quarters. Sorry, Rams. NFL games are 4 quarters long, and these Denver Broncos live and breathe it. Especially in the rarefied air of their home field in front of the sold-out throng of Broncos Country. Sean Payton is still the head coach of this team. He has Davis Webb, Vance Joseph, and his players ready to do their jobs on game day. I’m not going to sit here and say this team doesn’t have flaws. We’re going to talk about them. I’m going to point out the same weaknesses we’ve been talking about on this team for at least a year, if not two. But I’m going to give praise where it is due and shout from the rooftops that this team is packed with winners. These guys believe in each other and their coaches. The coaches know how to make adjustments and help their players when things aren’t going to plan. Underestimate this Broncos team at your own peril, NFL. Offense This game was very Jekyll and Hyde from one half of the game to the other. The big problem with the first half is the same problem with these Denver Broncos over the past year when Sean Payton was calling plays. Davis Webb is starting darn near every drive early with a run. He’s then calling simple short passing plays mostly at or behind the line of scrimmage or within 5 yards of it. This is predictable, and teams have been largely burying the Broncos early in games because of how predictable the play calling is. The big problem is the pass game design and how they execute the plays early in games. For whatever reason, Bo Nix isn’t throwing downfield much at all early in games. That’s the one thing that Payton and Davis Webb need to change soon. This team is capable of putting teams away early; they just need to play football in the first half the way they do in the 2nd half, with more throws downfield in the play designs being executed by the offense. I think it is worth noting that this problem can be play call and design, or it can be player execution. It is largely impossible for us as fans to understand, looking from the outside. We do not know what the call is, what options exist for the quarterback to execute, and what reads are being made that dictate where the ball needs to go. I’m just saying that whatever the cause, this offense is limited by this very obvious trend early in games that we’ve seen both this season and last season. When the 2nd half came around (starting with our 2nd drive in the 3rd quarter), the team finally started leaning on the run game. I’ll point out that the running game wasn’t even terribly successful. That part doesn’t matter. The team often got to 2nd and 7ish, then 3rd and 4 or 5. These are much more manageable downs than 3rd and 7 or more. Webb needs to be braver about running the rock more often early in the games. This should not constantly be a 2nd-half adjustment to play calling. Quarterbacks Bo Nix absolutely has ice water running in his veins. He thrives on being backed into a corner with the odds stacked against him. It can be maddening to watch him derp through half of a football game only to turn into Superman in the 2nd half, but those of us in Broncos Country that have been watching since the 80s or before are kinda used to this brand of football. We’ve got some critiques of Nix to talk about, but the baseline is that I love this player and what he brings to this football team. There is no quarterback in the NFL today I would rather have on my team than Nix, full stop. So let’s not forget that Nix is a young NFL quarterback. He’s showing it with some of his choices where he’s locking onto one route and throwing it regardless of what is in front of his eyes. He should have had two more interceptions in this game from throws that should have just gone into the stands. Hopefully he’s getting coached to know his limits (the end zone bomb attempt to Sutton that came up far short when he was throwing off his back foot moving to his right) and read defensive leverage and know when your guy is owned (he had another one of these poor throws tonight that was dropped). The interesting thing is that his one recorded interception in this game was from being hit, not necessarily making a bad throw. Back to the positives: His 2-point conversion to Waddle was an absolutely filthy, undefendable dime. You can not throw a pass more perfectly on and out and up to the back of the end zone than what he did there. His touchdown to Bryant was also smartly placed high so that his receiver could high point it and shield it from being batted down. Line Quinn Meinerz absolutely embarrassed Aaron Donald by getting him going sideways, lifting him off the ground, and throwing him down for a pancake block. Meinerz is an All-Pro guard still. Interestingly, after this, Donald didn’t line up much across from Meinerz. Also, suspiciously, Meinerz got texted about being drug tested following the game . McGlinchey costs us our first drive, getting worked into Nix’s lap. To his credit, he was a key blocker who got pulled out to the flat to help Bo get us down to 1st and goal at the ½ yard line. He played that to perfection and did a great job blocking for Bo. Running Backs RJ Harvey may not have done much in the run game (2 runs for 6 yards), but his catches out of the backfield were money. He led all receivers with 6 catches for 41 yards. His play as a joker even set up the big pass to Bryant later in the game, where a defensive back crashed down to stop Harvey, leaving Bryant wide open with no defenders in 20 yards. JK Dobbins was a dependable runner for the Broncos this game. He had 17 rushes for a paltry 49 yards, but he kept the offense in manageable situations. He did get lucky on his fumble with the ball bouncing directly into Bryant’s hands. He looks like a dinged-up player to me (which he likely is with a sore hammy). I’d still like to see more than a 6-yard gain as his best out of 17 attempts. Tyler Badie needs some love for all the work he’s doing for this team. Sure, he only ran once for 2 yards. But he had a superb route out of the backfield for a 10+ play on 2nd and 10. More importantly, he was in on many of our obvious passing situations as a pass blocker. Receivers Pat Bryant absolutely slayed and honestly should get more targets. His touchdown catch was not an easy catch to make, and he went up and got the score. He also absolutely bailed the team out of a 2nd and 20 with a crossing route wide open for a huge gain. He also had his defender beat on an out route on the final drive, got bumped to draw a pass interference flag late in the game. And for the record, yes, that was pass interference. Section 5 of the officiating handbook, article 2: “Initiating contact with an opponent by shoving or pushing off, thus creating separation.” The defender shoved Bryant in the back, which is what the flag was for. When you slow-mo the end of the play, it looks like no big deal. The problem is that most of the Los Angeles Rams fans and other ass hats in the media (including Collinsworth and their hack ref from the announcing crew for Sunday Night Football) aren’t looking at the whole play. They are cherry-picking the end in slow-mo instead of watching the whole play. Cortland Sutton had a pretty up-and-down game. He only hauled in 3 of his 7 targets for 46 yards. But man, were two of those catches important. He made our first first down out of sheer grit. He ran a go on the sideline, got interfered with, and still fought…

title: NFL Power Rankings for Week 4: Denver Broncos enter the top five after yet another comeback win
summary: The Denver Broncos have earned a reputation for being the comeback kings of the NFL after doing it in back-to-back weeks. They won so many of those types of games last season that most assumed they would be due for a reversion to the mean in 2026. So far, that hasn’t been the case. This […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 27: Pat Bryant #13 of the Denver Broncos makes a catch for a touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams during the third quarter at Empower Field At Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Tafoya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos have earned a reputation for being the comeback kings of the NFL after doing it in back-to-back weeks. They won so many of those types of games last season that most assumed they would be due for a reversion to the mean in 2026. So far, that hasn’t been the case. This team thrives off the high pressure, high stakes of a comeback. The power rankings are a mixed bag because of that. They rose across the board, but some prognosticators only moved them slightly still doubting their ability to keep up the comeback game. However, plenty do believe and the move was significant and into the Top 5 overall. Frankly, I don’t know if they can keep this up. But I do know I’m enjoying the ride and enjoying the Bo Nix experience. It’s not quite like Tebow Time. It’s a lot more like John Elway with a hint of Tebow, because some of these comebacks are just too insane not to think of Tebow. Here’s how the Broncos are doing in this week’s power rankings around the web: CBS Sports – 6th Coming back to win games late is their calling card. They did it again against the Rams Sunday night, but that’s playing with fire on a weekly basis. NBC Sports – 4th The Rams let the Broncos hang around just long enough to steal it. ESPN – 6th The Broncos’ offensive struggles, especially in first halves, have dragged down everybody’s numbers. They haven’t found a rhythm much of the time, and save for Jaylen Waddle’s 138-yard effort against the Jaguars in Week 2 , the WRs have been caught up in the wash (Pat Bryant has the group’s only TD catch). Sutton, who is second in targets to Waddle with 16, could be seen as the biggest disappointment. He has yet to eclipse more than 10 fantasy points in any game. New York Times – 4th Bo Nix is 26-11 as Denver’s starter, which gives him eight more wins than any other member of the 2024 quarterbacks class. So Broncos fans aren’t interested in hearing about how he’s 30th in the league in EPA per dropback (minus-0.14) and 26th in touchdown-to-interception ratio (4-to-3). Denver scored as many points in the second half Sunday as it did in the first 10 quarters of the season combined, so maybe Nix and offensive coordinator Davis Webb are figuring each other out. USA Today – 5th They’ve been 10 points better on the scoreboard every week, meaning they’re on pace to score 40 at San Francisco on Sunday. Maybe. Yet for all the scrutiny that’s followed new OC Davis Webb, it’s the defense that’s really underachieved here so far. A team that averaged four sacks per game in 2025 is currently at 2.67. Fox Sports – 3rd They had a second half for the ages against the Rams, maybe with a little help from the officials. If they could just get QB Bo Nix and their offense going a little sooner, they’d be a scary team. But they certainly have the defense to play against anyone, and Sean Payton may be the best coach in the NFL when his team is playing from behind. They’ve already come from behind twice to win this year. And yes, I know they were blitzed by the Chiefs in Week 1, and they are still ranked ahead of them. These are power rankings, not standings. Thanks for your continued concern. What do you think of these power rankings? Share in the comments section below!

title: Bo Nix may struggle early, but he is proving to be the comeback king of the NFL
summary: Through 37 regular season games with the Denver Broncos, there haven’t been many fast starts for third year quarterback Bo Nix. That usually ends up crippling a team’s ability to find a way to win. However, Nix’s second half heroics and elevated play in the game’s waning moments have been a constant through his career. […]
full_text: Sep 27, 2026; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams during the second half at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Through 37 regular season games with the Denver Broncos, there haven’t been many fast starts for third year quarterback Bo Nix. That usually ends up crippling a team’s ability to find a way to win. However, Nix’s second half heroics and elevated play in the game’s waning moments have been a constant through his career. Last night’s performance certainly wasn’t Nix’s best game. Not by a long shot. Nevertheless, he and his teammates on the offensive side of the ball performed much better in the second half and were able to notch three scoring drives to help the team find a way to win. With Denver’s comeback victory against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football , Nix is now 26-11 as the starting quarterback for the Broncos dating back to the 2024 season. In that timeframe, he has ten fourth quarter comebacks and twelve game winning drives. That’s the most of any quarterback in the National Football League. After the game, Nix spoke to the media about how he and the rest of his teammates are able to defy the odds and find a way to put it all together when it matters most. “I think we’ve just been there and done that. Yes, we got down in a 16-point deficit, in a hole there, but we knew it was just a two-possession game with a couple of two-point conversations that we were able to convert on. That was obviously huge,” stated Nix. “Overall, it may not look pretty, may not play a great second half in the future, but that’s why you play a good, complete four-quarter game. As a team, you put it all together. Then that’s just what we did. We kept battling and did what it took to get the win.” Nix is no stranger to adversity. In his time at Auburn, he had his fair share of ups and downs. While he carved out several huge victories in his time with the Tigers, they never won a bowl game and endured two losing seasons with him at the helm of their offense. After their 6-7 finish in 2021, Nix transferred to Oregon with the hope he could revive his collegiate career. Nix was a sub-60 percent passer at Auburn but elevated his passing game to new heights with the Ducks. In his two seasons in Eugene, Nix put up two monster seasons and had some of the best passing production of any quarterback in the nation. He would finish his collegiate career with the most games ever played and started by a quarterback. Through all the ups and downs, his experience and gridiron journey resulted in him being picked at the twelfth overall selection by the Broncos in the 2024 NFL Draft. Fast forward to the present day, and Nix has arguably been the best quarterback of his class that featured six signal callers picked in the first round. The slow starts might be rough to watch, but the end result usually winds up in Denver’s favor by finishing strong. “For us, once you’ve done it once, you feel like you can do it again. It’s just kind of where we are. We have a great belief that fourth quarter, end of game we’re going to have the ball last and no matter what, we’re going to go down and hopefully do whatever it takes to win the game or if not, tie the game and let our defense go out there and keep the game going. I think it’s just an overall belief, a team belief. When we get in the huddle, you don’t see any flinching in anybody’s eyes,” added Nix. While he still has a lot to work on to make that big Year 3 jump, there is no doubting Nix’s mental toughness and intangibles. When the game is on the line, he finds a way to rise to the occasion and lead his team to victory. He is the definition of clutch. He has the ‘it’ factory you can’t teach. It may not always be pretty to start things off, but the team and all of Broncos Country will gladly take the wins. At the end of the day, winning is what matters. And folks, Bo Nix is a winner, and I believe a quarterback who is just scratching the surface of his overall potential.

title: Horse Tracks: Are come-from-behind wins sustainable?
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Since the Broncos’ thrilling come-from-behind (way behind) win over the Rams Sunday night, all the Monday morning talk highlighted the “unsustainability” of winning like this. But is it? Down 16-0 at halftime to the Rams, the Broncos did what the Broncos do — came up with an unlikely win after some […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - SEPTEMBER 27: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos celebrates a touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams during the fourth quarter at Empower Field At Mile High on September 27, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Since the Broncos’ thrilling come-from-behind (way behind) win over the Rams Sunday night, all the Monday morning talk highlighted the “unsustainability” of winning like this. But is it? Down 16-0 at halftime to the Rams, the Broncos did what the Broncos do — came up with an unlikely win after some miracle plays. Like, two touchdowns, two two-point conversions, a Talanoa Hufanga pick-six, a couple fortunate penalty calls and finally Bo Nix leaping over the goal line with 47 seconds left for the win. All of it in the second half and much of it in the fourth quarter. “For us, once you’ve done it once, you feel like you can do it again,” Nix said. “It’s just kind of where we are.” In fact, the Broncos’ 30-26 victory was the first time in franchise history that Denver rallied from double-digit deficits in the second half two weeks in a row. That 30-point rally at Mile High followed last week’s 14-point fourth-quarter pickup to beat the Jaguars after being down 13-3 early in the third quarter. “They’re one of the best teams in football, and I think they have one of the most clutch quarterbacks in football.” — @danorlovsky7 on the Denver Broncos and Bo Nix after their comeback win against the Rams 😤 pic.twitter.com/uQkvt6316o — First Take (@FirstTake) September 28, 2026 Courtland Sutton pointed out that this kind of pressure to win either “makes diamonds or busts a pipe.” And anyone whose been a Broncos fan for more than a minute knows the Broncos’ M.O. is to constantly teeter on that balance. Even the young guy, second-year receiver Pat Bryant, sees this as kind of “what they do.” “I honestly feel like it’s just [that] we’ve been in these situations before. [We] came in at halftime. Nobody really flinched. You know what I’m saying?” he said after the gaem. “We know the mistakes we made. We know what we need to correct. We went out there and performed how we needed to perform.” Interesting comparison For fun I did some rough calculations of fourth-quarter comebacks since 1978, the year often delineated for a shift to higher octane offenses, which was highlighted by the early 80s with the entrance of such gun-slingers as Dan Marino, Boomer Esiason and our favorite, John “The Duke” Elway. Since that time, the Broncos are tied with the Dolphins for second-most come-from-behind wins as a team at 104. So if like me, you’ve thought of the Broncos as seemingly always fighting back at the end of the game, you’d be right. Those of us who grew up in the Elway era basically expected wins based on fourth-quarter rallies. Throw in a few games like The Drive and you just don’t even flinch at a comeback. But personnel change and most teams don’t make it a habit to win in the last quarter. Unless you’re the Denver Broncos. Both Elway and Peyton Manning are among the top quarterbacks for most game-winning drives. Based on stats from Pro Football Reference for quarterbacks since 1978, Tom Brady leads for most regular season wins after trailing by one score in the fourth quarter at 46. Manning is second with 43 and Elway ninth at 31. But those guys played a lot of games. For fun I looked at Elway’s come-from-behind victories in his first 37 games, the number of pro football contests Nix has played. And I bet you can guess who has more. Nix has 10 and Elway had six – one as a rookie in 1983, two in 1984 and three in the first 11 games of his third season in 1985. Elway’s 10th comeback win was in his 43rd game, the 1986 opener against the Raiders. Nix’s comeback wins derive from three his rookie season, five last year (including everyone’s favorite playoff win over the Bills) and then the two so far this season. "He seems unfazed with the idea that the offense is struggling. That is a great trait to have as a quarterback." @tthasselbeck joins @notthefakeSVP and reacts to Bo Nix's performance in the Broncos' win vs. the Rams 🏈 pic.twitter.com/Gvh2xBayLe — SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) September 28, 2026 So, maybe it is sustainable? Logic would say no. Basic odds would say unlikely. But the Broncos experience says, well, yeah maybe. To quote our recent UFGer, DNVRNortwoods, “F logic.” And you have to because the Broncos continually defy it. “I think it’s just us gaining our feet underneath us and realizing where we’re at,” Riley Moss said of the comeback win. “It’s ebbs and flows, right? You’ve got to be able to bounce back when things don’t go your way, and that’s what we did. Towards the end of the game, they drove down [the field] a little bit, but we were able to bend and not break and finish it off.” A common theme from Nix and his teammates after the game was that “they’ve been there before.” Once you stack comeback wins, the next one doesn’t seem impossible. “In the huddle, I feel a lot of belief and know that we’ve been there before. We have what it takes to go down against a really good defense and score points,” Nix said, adding that he’ll probably never “play the perfect game,” so being resilient and just ready to make the next play better is all they can do. And he pushed back on the idea that the Broncos need to be trailing to find another gear. Most games come down to the last possession anyway. “The more important thing is we’re winning these games when it comes down to it and we’re not losing,” he added. “I think we’ve just been there and done that.” Talanoa Hufanga became the first player in Broncos history (and just the 5th in NFL history) to have these in a single game. 1 sack 2 INTs 1 pick six Historic game for Huf. pic.twitter.com/W2KFNOmRF5 — Zac Stevens (@ZacStevens) September 28, 2026 And when the Broncos were down 16-0, Nix and his teammates just looked at it as being down a couple scores rather than focusing on how poorly they were playing in the first half. “As a team, you put it all together. Then that’s just what we did,” Nix said. “We kept battling, and kept battling and did what it took to get the win.” Talanoa Hufanga, who was largely responsible for the comeback thanks to a timely pick-six and the game-sealing interception in the end zone, said he was talking to fellow safety Brandon Jones on the sidelines about the second-half atmosphere reminding him of playing under the Friday night lights in high school. “Sometimes you make [the game] too much. You put the pressure on yourself to play more than what you’re capable of, but I really just came out there and felt like it was just a kids game today in a high school game, and it felt like a super real feeling,” Hufanga said. But that doesn’t mean the head coach and players don’t realize that there isn’t always time for a comeback, so starting faster is a major improvement goal. “I’m comfortable with the grit of a team that can play well in the fourth quarter,” Payton said. “I’m uncomfortable with how we play at the start of games, if that’s a fair answer.” Still, the team has belief, and that will win a lot of games because they maintain poise and focus. “It’s pretty inspiring, the fight that we have and the willingness to go out there and compete,” said Pat Surtain II. “No matter how far we’re down, no matter what the game is looking like, we always find a way to come back and find a way to win. That’s what’s important in this game —finding ways to win.” Amen and hallelujah.
author: Laurie Lattimore-Volkmann

title: Survey: Will the Lions beat the Panthers in Week 4?
summary: Throughout the offseason, SB Nation will host NFL fan surveys, sponsored by FanDuel Sportsbook. For Pride of Detroit, we are tasked with fielding questions from Detroit Lions fans, and as we head into Week 4 of the 2026 NFL season, we have two questions for fans this week: After returning to their winning ways by […]
full_text: Oct 8, 2023; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) throws a pass against the Carolina Panthers in the first quarter at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con Throughout the offseason, SB Nation will host NFL fan surveys, sponsored by FanDuel Sportsbook . For Pride of Detroit, we are tasked with fielding questions from Detroit Lions fans, and as we head into Week 4 of the 2026 NFL season, we have two questions for fans this week: Will the Lions beat the Panthers in Week 4? (weekly question) Are you confident the Lions are headed in the right direction? (recurring poll) After returning to their winning ways by defeating the Jets in Week 3, the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook believe Detroit will stay on the winning track in Week 4 against the Panthers, having set the original betting line at Lions -2.5 points and shifting it to -3.5-points in recent days . Under head coach Dave Canales, the Panthers have shown growth, going from a 5-12 football team to an 8-9 division winner. While the Panthers have started the season 1-2, they have built a low-key solid roster, but unfortunately, they’ve been hit hard by the injury bug. In addition to replacing both starting offensive tackles due to injuries/illness this offseason, they’ve also had to place 2025 second-round pick EDGE Nic Scourton and 2026 third-round pick WR Chris Brazell on injured reserve. Currently, prized free agent linebacker Devin Lloyd (calf), starting safety Nick Scott (rib), and starting wide receiver Xavier Legette (knee) are dealing with injuries that kept them from playing last week, while several other starters were injured in Week 3, including corner Jaycee Horn (quad), corner Mike Jackson (groin), wide receiver Jalen Coker (quad/ankle), left guard Damien Lewis (UCL), and quarterback Bryce Young (lower body). Horn and Lewis are expected to be unavailable this week, but several others could also miss this game against the Lions. The Lions are dealing with their own significant injuries, but the Panthers’ potential absences could help the Lions score 31 points for the fourth game in a row. The Panthers have shown the firepower to put up lots of points, and a banged-up Lions secondary will certainly help, but they may need to keep pace while missing several key pieces. full_text: DETROIT, MI - DECEMBER 04: Graham Glasgow #60 of the Detroit Lions runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at Ford Field on December 4, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tuesday’s NFL transaction list featured a lot of familiar names and an interesting tryout for the Detroit Lions. To begin with, two former Lions centers earned a tryout for the Baltimore Ravens: Graham Glasgow and Kingsley Eguakun. Glasgow is a 10-year veteran who started 14 games for the Lions at center last year, but Detroit cut him in a salary cap saving move , and the former Michigan Wolverine has not signed anywhere since. Eguakun started a couple of games for the Lions last year, his second season with Detroit. However, toward the end of the season, he was poached by the Browns off of Detroit’s practice squad. He failed to make the Browns’ final roster this year, then spent a couple weeks on the Giants’ practice squad. The Ravens failed to re-sign Tyler Linderbaum this offseason, choosing to rely on veteran Danny Pinter instead. Unfortunately, Pinter suffered a season-ending injury during the preseason, leaving the job to Jovaughn Gwyn. But in Week 3 both Gwyn and his backup, Ethan Pocic, suffered long-term injuries, leaving the Ravens with a huge hole at center. As for the Lions, they worked out wide receiver Lawrence Keys on Tuesday. If that name sounds familiar, he was one of the four UFL receivers Detroit signed this offseason , along with Tay Martin, Tarik Black, and Lucky Jackson. Keys never really got a chance to make the Lions’ roster, as he was cut with an injury settlement in early August. Now it appears the duration of his injury settlement has elapsed and Detroit may be interested in continuing his development. Or they simply could be checking in on his health from a hamstring injury. In other Lions-related news, former Detroit safety Tracy Walker saw his suspension lifted from an unknown infraction. Walker received a 12-game suspension for the 2025 season, then another three-game suspension for 2026. He has not been employed by an NFL team since a brief stint on the 49ers practice squad in 2024. Additionally, former Lions guard Kevin Zeitler visited with the Packers on Tuesday, as Green Bay tries to solve their offensive line issues.

title: NFL Week 4 power rankings: Confidence in Jared Goff has Detroit Lions on the rise
summary: In Week 3, the Detroit Lions (2-1) took on a New York Jets team that was sporting one of the best defenses in the NFL to start the 2026 season. After landing near the top of most defensive statistical categories, the Jets looked like a much bigger challenge than the Lions had faced. Yet, when […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) waves at fans after 31-24 win over New York Jets at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co In Week 3, the Detroit Lions (2-1) took on a New York Jets team that was sporting one of the best defenses in the NFL to start the 2026 season. After landing near the top of most defensive statistical categories, the Jets looked like a much bigger challenge than the Lions had faced. Yet, when the lights came on at Ford Field in Detroit, quarterback Jared Goff was once again stellar, leading the Lions to 400 total yards of offense (more than the Jets allowed in their previous games combined) and scoring 31 points for the third game in a row. While the Lions’ defense is still a major question mark and needs improvement, most national analysts believe Goff and his supporting cast—most notably Jahmyr Gibbs—are playing at such a high level that the Lions can outscore most other teams. As a result, the Lions are moving up, or staying neutral, in this week’s national power rankings. Let’s take a closer look. The Athletic: 6 (Previous rank: 8) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : QB confidence: Should be higher If former Lions defensive coordinator Aaron Glen thought he was going to rattle Jared Goff, he was sorely mistaken. The New York Jets blitzed Goff 16 times Sunday, and the 31-year-old was 16-for-16 for 173 yards and two touchdowns on those plays. For the season, he has five touchdowns, no interceptions and a completion percentage of 86.7 when blitzed, according to TruMedia. Overall, he leads the league in touchdown passes (eight) and hasn’t thrown a pick. USA Today: 10 (Previous rank: 10) From Nate Davis : How consistent has this offense been? Exactly 31 points in every game. A low of 355 yards and a high of 381. And just one turnover. If a defense that’s allowed the most points (95) in the league can hold on long enough to get some reinforcements, this team has a legit shot at finally ending the league’s longest hex of failing to qualify for the Super Bowl. Sporting News: 11 (Previous rank: 14) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions need every bit of what Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs are doing to light it up offensively with their defense porous in every which way. Shootouts follow everywhere they go and they might need to make a drastic change soon. CBS Sports: 12 (Previous rank: 15) From Pete Prisco : Jahmyr Gibbs is carrying this team and is in the early MVP conversation. They have to be happy to be 2-1 with all the defensive injuries. Yahoo Sports: 13 (Previous rank: 13) From Frank Schwab : The Lions have given up the most points and second-most yards in the NFL this season. They beat the Jets on Sunday but allowed 335 yards and 24 points. Two Jets, Garrett WIlson and Kenyon Sadiq, had 100-yard receiving games. Most Lions games this season will be high scoring. They’ll need the defense to make a few plays, like it did in the final minute. The Jets reached the Lions’ 28-yard line, but safety Chuck Clark sacked Geno Smith on a blitz, causing a fumble that the Lions recovered. “And then for our defense to have to, man, they had to make that stop,” Lions head coach Campbell said. “That’s what it was going to come down to. And it was such a great call by [defensive coordinator] Kelvin Sheppard and those guys executing it.” ESPN: 13 (Previous rank: 14) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Fantasy surprise: QB Jared Goff It’s sometimes easy to forget about Goff’s consistency because he plays alongside elite playmakers such as RB Jahmyr Gibbs and WR Amon-Ra St. Brown. The veteran QB is a viable starter in fantasy this season, averaging 21.9 points. Goff was the 18th-best quarterback in our draft rankings and had an ADP of 131.4. After Sunday’s win, Gibbs lauded Goff as Detroit’s “leader.” “We trust him with everything,” Gibbs said. NFL.com: 14 (Previous rank: 13) From Nick Shook : We know the Lions can put up points in bunches by leaning heavily on Jahmyr Gibbs, and this offense is capable of keeping them in every game they play. Their defensive struggles in the fourth quarter remain concerning, even if a takeaway saved them from another trip to overtime. Sports Illustrated: 14 ( Previous rank: 18) From Connor Orr : Jared Goff is one of six quarterbacks in NFL history to start the season with more than 800 yards passing and eight touchdowns in three games. If the Lions can go out and get themselves Joey Porter, all will be right in the world, as the offense is holding up its end of the bargain.

title: Lions vs. Jets Song of the Game: ‘Dashboard’ by Modest Mouse
summary: After a brief hiatus, “Song of the Game” has returned, back by popular demand of our Editor in Chief and Sticktator, Jeremy Reisman. While I’ve been absolutely swamped between work, writing/editing, podcasting, being a husband and a parent, the next half hour I’ll spend writing this is a welcome break of such serious bellyaching about […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Head Coach Aaron Glenn of the New York Jets congratulates Head Coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions with their 31-24 win after the game at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a brief hiatus, “Song of the Game” has returned, back by popular demand of our Editor in Chief and Sticktator, Jeremy Reisman. While I’ve been absolutely swamped between work, writing/editing, podcasting, being a husband and a parent, the next half hour I’ll spend writing this is a welcome break of such serious bellyaching about the secondary. Lions vs. Jets Week 3 Song of the Game: “Dashboard” by Modest Mouse Growing up in the day and age of burning CDs to create the soundtrack of your bus rides to and from school, Modest Mouse was a staple of my collection. “Float On” and “Ocean Breathes Salty” spun a bunch on my Sony D-EJ360 Walkman . It hit me right in the midst of my percolating angst as middle school tested my place in the world, and Modest Mouse was just what the doctor ordered . “Dashboard” is the lead single from the band’s fifth studio album—a track guitarist and songwriter Johnny Marr, formerly of The Smiths, worked on during his first day riffing with Modest Mouse. It’s much more dance-driven pop rock than the slacker rock the band debuted with a decade prior, but even in a different flavor, it’s still damn good. Modest Mouse’s lineup has changed a bunch over the band’s life cycle, as has the Detroit Lions coaching staff over Dan Campbell’s six years as head coach. Aaron Glenn was one of my favorite hires Campbell made at the start of his tenure, and what he managed to accomplish as a defensive coordinator in 2024 was nothing short of remarkable. It led him to taking a head coaching position with the New York Jets the year after, and while it was a rocky start for the former Jets cornerback, he’s undoubtedly got that team in a position that feels eerily similar to the way Campbell had the Lions in 2022. They’re still feeling out the way to win, but they’re right there—and with tons of draft capital in this upcoming draft. Oh, it should’ve been, could’ve been worse than you would ever know Well, you told me about nowhere well it sounds like someplace I’d like to go Detroit’s defense is still very much a work in progress, especially on the backend, and that’s not something you want to hear about a football team through three weeks of regular season play. Many drew tired of Glenn’s unwillingness to spy mobile quarterbacks, and found him to be overaggressive by the end of his time in Detroit, and we’re seeing how any place other than where we’re at with this defense is someplace we’d like to see it go. Well, it would’ve been, could’ve been worse than you would ever know Oh, the dashboard melted, but we still have the radio And yet, with as bad as the defense has been—with the dashboard melted—we still have the Lions offense playing their same ol’ tunes. 31 points in three straight games, and this game would’ve been, could’ve been worse than you would ever know had it not been for this offense keeping this team in the win column. Well we scheme and we scheme but we always blow it We spent all week waiting to see the adjustments Kelvin Sheppard and the defense would make after getting embarrassed on “Thursday Night Football.” What sort of adjustments could they possibly make to clean up that mess? But up until the fourth quarter, the Lions held the Jets to just 10 points. Detroit had a comfortable 24-10 lead, they had schemed and schemed… but they ended up blowing that lead, letting the Jets tie the game with a little over four minutes remaining in the game. We’ve yet to crash, but we still might as well tow it Standing at a light switch to each east and west horizon Every dawn you’re surprising And in the evening one’s consoling Saying, “See it wasn’t quite as bad as.” Four plays later, the Lions have the lead, the defense forces a game-winning turnover, and I spent my op-ed this week reminding everyone that while the Lions’ dashboard is melted, we’ve yet to crash, and the radio’s still working, so we might as well enjoy it. If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016 , 2017 , 2018 , 2019 , 2020 , 2021 , 2022 . And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here .
