title: Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent? Bears face a QB decision
summary: Keenum stepped up in a big way against the Eagles, but Bagent is healthy and Ben Johnson won't reveal his QB1.
full_text:
CHICAGO -- Chicago Bears quarterback Case Keenum had about 30 minutes Monday night before the euphoria of leading a huge win over the Philadelphia Eagles met the reality of possibly heading back to the bench next week. It's a reality with which he is not unfamiliar.

 "We'll have a discussion as a coaching staff, and we'll see where we need to go from here," Bears coach Ben Johnson said after the 27-7 win. "But I said it last week, and I'll say it again, there was a reason why Tyson [Bagent] ended training camp as our No. 2 quarterback."

 Bagent had spent much of last week in concussion protocol and was active and on the sideline Monday. Caleb Williams was ruled out Saturday because of a hamstring injury.

 So Keenum, who hadn't started a regular-season in 1,009 days, stole the spotlight, completing 24-of-34 passes for 247 yards and two touchdowns.

 Now he might be in a backup role once again when the Bears host the New York Jets on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, Fox).

 In 2017, Keenum subbed in for Sam Bradford with the Minnesota Vikings after a recurring knee injury derailed Bradford after Week 1. Keenum went 11-3 in the regular season, and his game-winning TD pass to Stefon Diggs against the New Orleans Saints in the divisional playoff game is known as the Minneapolis Miracle. The Vikings lost to the Eagles in the NFC Championship Game.

 But even as the wins piled up that season, including an eight-game win streak, Keenum knew he was a game away from being back on the bench. Former Vikings coach Mike Zimmer was reluctant to name Keenum the team's full-time starter. He took it game by game and often delayed naming a starter until days before kickoff.

 Keenum learned to live with the uncertainty. As he's bounced from backup to starter to backup over his 15-year NFL career, he's learned to appreciate every opportunity.

 "This means a bunch to me, man," Keenum told his teammates postgame. "This was taken from me a lot of times. "And to have [Johnson] call me and bring me back, [helped me] find the love of the game again. To have my family, my kids get to watch me ... I'm telling you, we've got something special here." The Bears' win over the Eagles didn't require a miracle from Keenum. The 38-year-old quarterback was "extraordinary" in the eyes of Johnson, completing 71% of his passes for 247 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. He was not sacked and converted a quarterback sneak for a touchdown.

 The impact of Keenum's night is more than just a feel-good story. It's the type of performance that may give the Bears the best chance to continue to find wins while Williams works his way back. He is expected to be sidelined three to four weeks with a Grade 2 hamstring strain.

 Bagent had only one day of practice ahead of the Eagles' game while working his way through concussion protocol, which he did not clear until Sunday afternoon. Johnson did not believe it was fair to make Bagent start a game having not gotten the same quality of reps that Keenum had gotten throughout the week.

 So Bagent, who was active, stayed on the sideline.

 Keenum had his most passing yards in a game since the 2019 season. A heavy dose of play-action resulted with Keenum going 11-of-12 for 128 yards and eight first downs.

 He was perfect when blitzed (11-of-11, 145 yards, 2 TDs) and averaged 12.4 yards per attempt. As Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio cranked up the heat, Keenum did his best. He was pressured on 10 of 35 dropbacks (28.6%) and averaged 9.9 yards per attempt under pressure.

 

 He beat that pressure by getting the ball out quickly, averaging 2.41 seconds of release time, according to Next Gen Stats, and found the end zone twice. That was the fastest a Bears quarterback has gotten a pass off since Week 6 of the 2023 season.

 Coincidentally, that last time was when Bagent stepped in against the Vikings for an injured Justin Fields . Bagent would then start Chicago's next four games as the team went 2-2 during that stretch.

 Had it not been for a concussion, Bagent would have started against the Eagles. The team's belief in him is reflected in a two-year, $10 million contract that made him one of the higher-paid backups in the league.

 But Keenum went from QB3 to starter in a matter of days and delivered a win that raises questions of how the Bears should proceed.

 "[Keenum] knows where everyone's supposed to be on every single play, and so he's really quick to recognize coverage," Johnson said. "He knows why we're calling the play, what we're looking for, and if we're not getting that, he's accelerating through it extremely quickly. And so that's what you get when you're 15 plus years in this league, playing this position, you've seen it all."

title: Can the Broncos keep pulling off unlikely comeback victories?
summary: Somehow, the Broncos keep finding ways to overcome their slow first-half starts, pulling off frenetic second-half comeback wins -- including in Week 3 against the Rams.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- The Denver Broncos have found the most improbable comfort zone. This past Sunday night's 30-26 victory over the Los Angeles Rams was the fourth time in Sean Payton's three-plus-season tenure as head coach the Broncos have won a game in which they were behind 14 or more points in the second half.

 "This team rises," safety Talanoa Hufanga said.

 Quarterback Bo Nix added that team's high-wire dance "feels like our DNA."

 Hufanga and Nix's comments form a pushback against proven concepts like regression to the mean or the thought that past results don't guarantee future performance. And yet another comeback win might be rejecting the common-sense belief that the Broncos can't keep winning in this fashion.

 

 But this past Sunday was the 10th time since Nix was drafted in 2024 that the Broncos have produced a fourth-quarter comeback victory. And it marked the first time in franchise history the Broncos have had consecutive comeback wins in which they trailed by double-digits in the second half (Denver overcame a 10-point, third-quarter deficit to beat the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 2 ).

 The Broncos (2-1) have developed a reputation for being second-half escape artists. But as they get set to face the undefeated San Francisco 49ers (3-0) on the road Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Levi's Stadium, CBS ), how do they really feel about their current trend of overcoming lackluster first halves to win in late, dramatic fashion?

 Payton tried to add some perspective moments after the Rams win, saying that a start like the Broncos had against Los Angeles -- in which they were outgained 273-67 in the first half while falling behind 16-0 -- would be "something we're frustrated about later if we don't get it cleaned up." And "later" could mean as soon as Sunday, given 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy leads the NFL in QBR (93.8) and touchdown passes (nine) while throwing only one interception.

 The 49ers lead the league in offensive efficiency by a margin of more than 14 points over the second-place Buffalo Bills , who are closer to seventh place than they are to San Francisco. The Niners also lead the NFL in offensive expected points added (EPA) by a little more than 15 points, with the No. 2 team (Buffalo) being closer to No. 8 than it is to the 49ers. So, the Broncos, who have scored only 10 first-half points this season, would rather not be forced rely on a third straight escape act.

 "We'll look at the tape [of Sunday's win] and I'm sure and pull our hair out with some stuff," Payton said. "And be excited about some things, too"

 While it's not ideal, the Broncos can be excited about their ability to recover and thrive in seemingly hopeless situations. And the win over the Rams was among their most improbable.

 

 "I wouldn't say it's good to be familiar in those situations, but once you are in those situations, you're familiar and you have been in that environment before and you understand what it takes to overcome the situations," Broncos wide receiver Courtland Sutton said. "... It allows you to play free, play fast."

 Every one of the Broncos' two-touchdown-plus comebacks of the Payton era saw them facing a win probability of 6% or less in the second half. His very first win in Denver, a 31-28 victory at the Chicago Bears in Week 4 of the 2023 season, saw the Broncos facing a win probability of 1.3% when they were behind 28-7 with 4:11 left in the third quarter. But two Russell Wilson touchdown passes, a Jonathon Cooper fumble return for a touchdown and a 51-yard field goal by Wil Lutz allowed Denver to score the final 24 points.

 Nix got two wins on those big deficits last season. The first came in Week 5 at the defending Super Bowl champion Philadelphia Eagles , when the Broncos had only a 5.7% chance of victory when down 17-3 early in the third quarter. But Nix led two fourth-quarter touchdown drives to go with a 36-yard Lutz field goal for a 21-17 win . Two weeks later, the Broncos upped the ante. They entered the fourth quarter down 19-0 to the New York Giants  and were behind 26-8 with 10:14 left, giving Denver a 0.2% chance to win. The Broncos scored a franchise-record 33 fourth-quarter points to pull out a 33-32 victory .

 Sunday's game had similar vibes, as the Broncos scored 30 second-half points to win a game in which they ran 20 fewer offensive plays than the Rams. Denver's win probability was 6.9% at halftime and dipped to 6% early in the third quarter. But three Nix touchdowns -- two passing, one rushing -- and a 66-yard interception return for a touchdown by Hufanga allowed the Broncos to defy fate again.

 "Pretty inspiring the fight that we have, the willingness to compete no matter how far we're down," Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II said. "... No matter what the game looks like, we find a way to come back and win. That's what's important."

 

 When discussing their performance in comeback mode, most Broncos point to third-down conversions, turnovers and red-zone performance. But they also cite the defense's ability to get the most important stops and Nix's demeanor in the pressure situations, which leads to exemplary second-half play.

 "Bo? He's a dawg," wide receiver Jaylen Waddle said.

 Nix led the league last season with seven game-winning drives and was third in the league with 1,130 passing yards in the fourth quarter, trailing only the Bills' Josh Allen and the Dallas Cowboys ' Dak Prescott . Nix has two more game-winning drives this season, leading the NFL. His total QBR is 46.6 but jumps to 60.6 in the final period.

 "Having a guy like that in the quarterback room, that doesn't complain ... doesn't cry, doesn't whine, just comes out and encourages us," Broncos wide receiver Pat Bryant said. "It's great."

 While the Broncos would like to start games better than they have and not need the dramatics, they take comfort in knowing that they're capable of rising to the occasion when pushed to the brink.

 "How do you respond?'' Sutton said. "... I think the more times you see that happen, I think it gives you the confidence that you can make a diamond out of a pressurized situation."

title: Can the 0-3 Texans defy history again to make playoffs?
summary: Houston became the first team in the common playoff format to make the postseason after starting 0-3 in 2025.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Is it déjà vu for the Houston Texans ?

 The preseason Super Bowl contenders find themselves at 0-3 for the second straight year -- and the losses have come in similar fashion.

 Last year, the Texans' first three games were lost on the last drive, and this season, the same happened in two of the three weeks.

 Quarterback C.J. Stroud was sacked and fumbled inside the red zone on Houston's last drive against the Buffalo Bills in Week 1, and in Week 3, the Texans' defense allowed a game-winning field goal against the Indianapolis Colts  with 16 seconds remaining.  

 

 But Houston remains confident despite the frustration.

 "We've been here before," Stroud said after the latest loss. "We can get these fixed, and we will." 

 Like last season, Houston's offense hasn't been great. The unit is averaging 18 points (tied for 23rd) and 326 yards (14th in total offense). Stroud also has been sacked 10 times, tied for second most in the NFL.

 They might have been able to circumvent history last year, but even that was a tall task. Entering this season, 25 teams had started 0-3 under the current playoff format (since 2020), and last year's Texans are the only one to reach the postseason, according to ESPN Research. Houston also became the seventh team in the Super Bowl era (1966) to reach the playoffs after 0-3, and the last team to do it before that was ... the 2018 Texans.

 "In this league, no one cares about what happened," Stroud said. "They just want to see if you won or lost. So at the end of the day, we know who we are in our locker room. We know we will hear noise all week.

 "But at the end of the day, it's us in the locker room."

 The Texans started 3-5 last season before winning their final nine games, but slow starts have become a trend for Houston under coach DeMeco Ryans. In Ryans and Stroud's debut season in 2023, the Texans started 0-2. The only anomaly under Ryans is 2024, when they started 2-0. 

 

 Still, the Texans have found a way to climb out of those holes -- reaching the divisional round of the playoffs during the past three years. But Ryans won't lean on past experiences because he believes each year is different.

 "For me, if we're 0-3, obviously I haven't coached good enough," Ryans said. "So, haven't coached good enough. I've got to coach better. If I coach better, we'll find ourselves on the winning side."

 The offense has sorely missed Pro Bowl wideout Nico Collins , who had seven catches for 75 yards and a TD in the opener. After compiling 381 yards in the opener, Houston has averaged 298.5 yards (23rd) and scored 11.5 points (tied for 30th) without Collins (hamstring). 

 Last year through three weeks, Houston's offense averaged 12.7 points (last), but its defense allowed 17 points (tied for fifth best). And while the defense gave up 36 points in Week 1 to the Bills, it has allowed 19.5 points (tied for 11th) and 283 yards per game (eighth fewest). The defense also has the fourth-best success rate (33%), the second-most sacks (nine), ranks third in tackle for loss rate (11.5%), sixth in yards per play (4.4) and fifth in quarterback pressure rate (22.1).

 But an alarming issue for the Texans has been their run game. The offensive line has allowed running backs David Montgomery and Woody Marks to be hit at the line of scrimmage 66.7% (the highest by eight points) on carries, according to Next Gen Stats. The unit has missed right guard Ed Ingram , who has missed the past two weeks with a groin injury, but a 33% stuff rate (the highest against) isn't sustainable for an effective run offense.

 Montgomery and Marks average minus-.3 yards a carry before contact, the lowest in the league -- which might be a telling story as to why Houston has the lowest rushing yards from running backs (33 per game).

 

 Stroud said there's "no excuses" for how they've performed, and Ryans believes they are working to improve things despite the alarming statistics. 

 "We're looking at everything from an offensive standpoint of the running game," Ryans said. "What can we do differently for us to make sure we can turn out some yards in a run game. The guys have to keep working. Have to keep trying to do some different things as well schematically with our run game. We just keep pressing forward. But we're headed in the right direction. We just have to clean up a few things."

 Despite the rough start, ESPN's Football Power Index still gives Houston a 22.4% chance to make the playoffs (the highest of the five remaining winless teams), but to avoid trying to have to defy history -- since 1990, only the 1992 Seattle Seahawks have made the playoffs after starting 0-4 -- a win over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, CBS) would be a good starting point.

 All-Pro defensive end  Will Anderson Jr ., drafted one spot after Stroud, believes the Texans are trending toward a turnaround.

 "We're heading in the right direction," said Anderson, who had 2.5 sacks Sunday. "What would the NFL be without adversity, and it sucks that we had to start this way again. But we're built for it. We have to keep chopping wood."

title: Why Geno Smith's hot start has been a bright spot for the Jets
summary: Despite being 1-2, the 35-year-old QB is completing over 75% of his passes.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- When the New York Jets traded for Geno Smith in March, bringing him back to where he started his career in 2013, it prompted a loud groan from their quarterback-scarred fanbase.

 Smith 1.0 doesn't evoke fond memories for Jets fans, and his performance last season for the Las Vegas Raiders was so uneven that the franchise was willing to eat $16 million of his 2026 salary to have him play elsewhere.

 Desperate for a bridge starter, the Jets took on the reclamation project, hoping he could recapture his Seattle Seahawks form -- circa 2022 when he led passers with over 100 attempts in completion percentage (69.8) -- and provide stability at their most unstable position.

 Through three games, Smith, 35, has exceeded expectations in New York, giving off early comeback-season vibes.

 

 "He's a warrior, man," tight end Jeremy Ruckert said. "He's a field general. We have the utmost confidence in him."

 Smith's completion rating (75.5%) ranks second in the NFL, and he's giving credence to the slogan, "What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas" -- which is to say, he's not throwing interceptions like he did as a member of the Raiders.

 After a league-high 17 interceptions last season, Smith has yet to throw one in 102 pass attempts. The last time he went three straight games without a pick was the final three games of the 2023 season, his second year as the Seahawks' starter.

 There's a lot of season left, but it's worth noting that Smith is putting up numbers that would rank among the best passing seasons in franchise history.

 Disclaimer: It's not a glittering history. Beyond franchise icon Joe Namath, there's only a sprinkling of above-average to excellent seasons over the last half-century.

 Only two players passed for 3,000 yards, 20 touchdowns and a 65% completion rate in the same season -- Chad Pennington (2002) and Brett Favre (2008). Mind you, these aren't extraordinary benchmarks. In today's NFL, they represent a solid season. In Favre's case, he had as many touchdown passes (22) as interceptions, which blemishes his season.

 With 783 yards and four touchdowns, Smith is on pace to blow away those marks. Of course, perspective is important.

 Smith has battled inconsistency at times in his career, and his current supporting cast is banged up. The status of running back Breece Hall (quad), wide receiver Adonai Mitchell (finger) and tight end Mason Taylor (thumb) are uncertain as they prepare to face the Chicago Bears on Sunday at Soldier Field. Chances are, he won't have Hall, a blow to an already sputtering rushing attack.

 That said, Smith has emerged as one of the early bright spots in the Jets' 1-2 start. On Sunday, he passed for 321 yards and three touchdowns in the 31-24 loss to the Detroit Lions , the first Jets' quarterback since Mike White in 2022 to have 300 yards and three touchdowns in a game.

 

 Coach Aaron Glenn praised Smith for "delivering the ball with confidence," staying in the flow of the offensive scheme and handling pass rushers in his face. Without Mitchell and Taylor, he still connected with eight different receivers, with 14 of his 31 completions going to tight ends. He also found Garrett Wilson on a consistent basis (10 receptions for 107 yards), something he didn't do in the first two games.

 "Are there some things that he has to improve on? Absolutely, absolutely he does, and he would tell you that himself," Glenn said of Smith. "But I think, overall, I was really pleased on how he operated."

 Smith's one mistake was a sack-fumble on the Jets' last possession, from the Lions' 28-yard line. He took the blame for the turnover, his first of the season. Glenn said, "He has to be able to hold on to the ball in that situation, so we can have another opportunity."

 Otherwise, he was almost perfect in the fourth quarter, completing 15 of 17 passes for 156 yards. Smith had more passing yards in that one quarter than Justin Fields produced in five of his nine starts last season.

 "He makes it easy to play receiver," said rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq , who had his first NFL touchdown reception Sunday.

 Smith will be a free agent after the season, and he knows that his chances of remaining a starter in the league will hinge on how he performs with the Jets. Maybe they will ask him back as a transition quarterback, holding the spot while they groom a highly drafted rookie.

 He hasn't talked about his future, though he acknowledged in spring that a triumphant comeback with the Jets, the team that drafted him 13 years ago, "would be like a story in a movie, right? Kind of like one of those superhero movies."

 It's still early in production, but the first few scenes look promising.

title: Inside George Kittle's 243-day recovery from torn Achilles
summary: Despite tearing his Achilles in the playoffs, Kittle appears to be back to his normal self. Here's how he won the recovery process.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- At 5:30 on a late March morning, eight weeks after surgery to repair his torn right Achilles, San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle was wide-awake.

 Kittle and a close group of friends had traveled to Bandon Dunes Golf Resort in Oregon for six rounds in four days. For 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk and others of the traveling party, it was a leisurely weekend on the links. For Kittle, it was an important step in his road back to the football field, a path he had defiantly proclaimed could have him ready for Week 1 in Melbourne, Australia. Which is why, when Juszczyk came downstairs to begin loosening up for that day's rounds, he found Kittle meticulously picking up a towel with his toes.

 It was a prime example of Kittle's disciplined approach to rehab his injured Achilles, and a side of Kittle the public rarely sees beneath the ebullient pro wrestling persona. This was the passionate, football-obsessed Kittle who had no desire to let anyone else author the timeline of his return.

 "It's fun to be doubted," Kittle, 32, told ESPN last week. "I'm not a chip-on-my-shoulder guy whatsoever, but when you have all the people who are like, 'Oh, you're not doing this, you're not doing that.' I'm like, 'I am doing that and extra. You believe whatever you want, you can talk however you want to talk, but when you see me Week 1, you can kick rocks.'"

 

 Kittle's discipline fueled an odds-defying, 243-day recovery from a torn Achilles suffered in a Jan. 11 NFC wild-card win over the Philadelphia Eagles . Through those eight months, he channeled his usual golden retriever energy into tedious daily rehab.

 The usual recovery can take anywhere from eight months to a year, and a June 2026 study done at Michigan State University and published in the Physician and Sportsmedicine Journal said only 27.1% of NFL players return to pre-injury performance levels. But so far this season, Kittle has reasserted himself as one of the league's best tight ends. After knocking off rust in the opener against the Rams, Kittle has posted 10 receptions for 162 yards and three touchdowns in the past two weeks -- second-most receiving yards among all tight ends over that span.

 Kittle's recovery required shuttling between physical therapists in Los Angeles (Heather Milligan) and Nashville (Jorge Rojas, DPT), as well as check-ins with the 49ers. With the guidance of Dr. Neil ElAttrache, the Los Angeles-based surgeon who performed the Achilles repair on Jan. 14, Kittle's team devised a blueprint to make his Week 1 dream a reality. Executing that plan was up to him.

 "As an athlete, you have to have that special sauce that you're really willing to push yourself to the very limit so that you can get back," Milligan said. "You don't wish injury on anybody, but the matchup of what it takes on this rehab with his personality and focus is a huge part of why he was so successful.

 "You've got the best patient in the world."

 
 THREE DAYS AFTER Kittle tore the Achilles, he laid on a surgical bed looking up at ElAttrache. He had two questions.

 The first, according to Kittle, was "Will I be healthy enough to make the golf trip to Bandon Dunes in eight weeks?" ElAttrache told him he "had a chance." Because Kittle's tear occurred high up near the soleus muscle, ElAttrache didn't have to drill into his heel, and the higher tear also allowed for superior blood flow to promote faster healing.

 The second question: "What are my chances of being back for Week 1?" Again, ElAttrache told Kittle it was possible. But he emphasized not to deviate from Milligan's instructions. "Once I was told that you have a shot, if you do all the things the right way, then I was like, 'All right, let's go,'" Kittle said. "I just attacked it with a super positive mindset."

 Upon meeting Milligan, Kittle got the rundown on how the recovery might go and what he had to do to make it successful. Milligan told Kittle about an athlete who came back from the same injury but had a huge difference in the size of his legs because he didn't properly strengthen both of them before returning to field work. That athlete tore the ACL on his other leg in his first year back.

 Kittle bought in immediately. Within minutes of getting his cast off, he was doing pointed toe flexes. Once he shed his walking boot, Milligan instructed him on which inserts to put in his shoes, starting with 3.5 centimeters. The inserts got smaller as he progressed, down to the 0.75 ones he still wears.

 

 Most importantly, Kittle never lost sight of the importance of strengthening both legs. Using numbers collected from the 49ers, Milligan and Rojas knew how strong Kittle was before the injury. To ensure the legs stayed within 10% strength of each other, Milligan tracked his calf girth and put him on a strain gauge to measure his raw toe-push force against a weight room floor plate.

 As Milligan emphasized, the goal wasn't just to get Kittle back on the field. It was to get him back as close to his normal level of performance as possible. That meant continuing to do the boring single leg heel raises or marble pickups for about 90 minutes to two hours every day over the course of 10 weeks.

 "When the strength is there, you cannot cheat that," Milligan said. "This is one injury. There is no way to skip steps. You just can't."

 
 WHEN THE NINERS began organized team activities in May, Kittle worked on an anti-gravity treadmill at 30% of his body weight. Two weeks later, Kittle was at 80% body weight. Soon after that, he was running on the football field at his home in Nashville, hitting 15 miles per hour.

 It was there that Kittle and Rojas worked through the most mind-numbing portions of the rehab. Since there are only so many exercises you can do on the Achilles -- calf raises off a wedge while standing, seated, with bands or with isolation holds -- Rojas tried to challenge Kittle by forcing him to do it all from different angles to best simulate some of the sudden football movements.

 Some days, Rojas threw Kittle tennis balls. Other days, they chatted about life, trying to find ways to break the boredom.

 All the while, Kittle was deploying his secret weapon: the BFR . A BFR is, essentially, a tourniquet that Kittle strapped to his thigh to cut off the blood flow into the muscles he was working. It tricks the brain into thinking it's taking on heavier loads than it actually is. According to Kittle, it's a better method to work to failure when you can't bear weight on the leg.

 In any Achilles recovery, the BFR is a suggested tool used a couple of times a week. Kittle used it twice every day.

 He also used the BFR as a recovery method, inflating it to 100% and then laying down for a few minutes so when he deflated it, the blood rushed back into the leg.

 "It's really hard," Rojas said. "It makes the easiest thing really challenging. It enabled us to push him hard from a muscular standpoint without putting a ton of stress on the Achilles that was healing ... Him really pushing through some of that boring stuff and pushing that calf to fatigue is why he was able to get back so fast."

 

 Most days, Rojas went to Kittle's house for workouts in his barn or on the field that serves as part of his backyard. As Kittle began running again, he goaded Rojas into joining him.

 One midsummer day, Rojas finally joined the run. Jogging at about 60% effort, Kittle left Rojas in the dust. Rojas knew then that Kittle was going to be back sooner than later.

 "George is one of one," Rojas said. "He physically is gifted, but there's a lot of guys who are as gifted, if not more so. For him, it's that mindset and the work ... I think that's the perfect recipe to get somebody back that quickly. And I don't think you see all of that dialed in on one person very often."

 
 BY EARLY JULY, Kittle had pushed himself through the early months of the recovery by picking up marbles with his toes while overlooking the ocean in Cabo San Lucas…
